sections.heading: NEON-MDF GTINX Microcontroller Development Framework
sections.text:
NEON-MDF is a firmware development kit for **GT32U2086**, providing peripheral
drivers, CMSIS, FreeRTOS and application examples. The SDK uses CMake/Ninja and
Arm GNU Toolchain, with terminal and VS Code workflows on Windows, Linux and macOS.

Each application is an independent project. The SDK generates device headers,
startup code, linker scripts and SVD from the GT32U2086 hardware description,
then packages firmware for programming through the UART BootROM.

[Environment setup](guide/Setup.md) · [Your first application](guide/FirstApp.md) ·
[Examples](examples/README.md) · [Documentation](guide/README.md)

sections.heading: What is included?
sections.text:
- **Peripheral drivers:** GPIO, UART, I2C, SPI, DMA, ADC, timer/PWM, RTC, watchdog,
  Flash/QSPI, CRC, TRNG and AES, plus clock/reset management and SYSCSR.
- **Application configuration:** select drivers and parameters with `menuconfig`/`sdkconfig`.
- **UART console:** `printf` for strings and integers, a programming tool and a serial monitor.
- **FreeRTOS:** Cortex-M0 port integration with application-specific heap/stack settings.
- **Examples and templates:** button inputs, GPIO outputs, interrupts, DMA and RTOS queues.

GT32U2086 has an Arm Cortex-M0 core running at up to 60 MHz, 512 KB instruction
Flash and 128 KB SRAM. FPGA examples typically configure a 10 MHz clock; set the
clock to match your hardware. Hardware details and firmware formats are covered
in the [GT32U2086 guide](guide/GT32U2086.md).

sections.heading: 1. Prepare the tools
sections.text:
| Tool | Requirement / purpose |
|---|---|
| Git | Obtain the SDK source |
| Arm GNU Toolchain | `arm-none-eabi` distribution with GCC, binutils and newlib |
| CMake | **3.25 or later**, for the SDK presets |
| Ninja | Build firmware |
| Python | **3.10 or later**, with packages from `neon-mdf/tools/requirements.txt` |
| USB–UART adapter and GT32U2086 board | Program and run firmware; no board is needed to build |

Install the tools using the [Windows, Linux or macOS setup guide](guide/Setup.md),
then verify them in your terminal:

```sh
arm-none-eabi-gcc --version
cmake --version
ninja --version
python3 --version
```

On Windows, use `python` if your Python installation does not provide `python3`.
VS Code and Node.js are only needed to use the editor or build/package its extension.

sections.heading: 2. Obtain the SDK and install Python packages
sections.text:
```sh
git clone https://github.com/ftel-cdc/neon_mdf.git
cd neon_mdf
python3 -m venv .venv
```

Activate the Python environment:

| Terminal | Command from `neon_mdf/` |
|---|---|
| Linux/macOS (Bash, Zsh) | `. .venv/bin/activate` |
| Windows PowerShell | `.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` |
| Windows CMD | `.venv\Scripts\activate.bat` |

```sh
python -m pip install -r neon-mdf/tools/requirements.txt
```

Keep this environment activated when configuring and building. Bundled examples
locate the SDK relative to their repository directory; see [creating an application](guide/FirstApp.md)
for projects outside the repository.

sections.heading: 3. Build your first firmware
sections.text:
Use `Printf_Log` to verify your environment and observe the firmware over UART:

```sh
cd examples/Printf_Log
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

The complete firmware image is **`build/GT32U2086/printf_log_image.bin`**. It
includes the BootROM header; select this file when programming an image manually.

sections.heading: 4. Program the board and view output
sections.text:
Connect the adapter TX to board RX, adapter RX to board TX, and share GND according
to your board schematic. Close any programs holding the serial port. Replace
`/dev/ttyUSB0` with your actual port, such as `COM3` on Windows or
`/dev/cu.usbserial-…` on macOS.

Run this command on **one line** from `examples/Printf_Log/`:

```sh
cmake -E env NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 NEON_MDF_SERIAL_BAUD=19200 cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target flash_uart_gt32u2086
```

Select **boot mode `100`**, wait for the tool to report that UART is ready, then
press **RESET**. Programming baud must match ROMCODE on your board; `19200` is the
example configuration. After successful programming, open the monitor:

```sh
cmake -E env NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 NEON_MDF_MONITOR_BAUD=19200 cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target serial_monitor
```

You should see `[INFO] counter=…` lines. Exit the monitor with `Ctrl+C`.
Select boot mode **`000`** to run the installed firmware after subsequent resets
or power cycles. See [UART programming](guide/GT32U2086Flashing.md) for connection
checks and troubleshooting.

sections.heading: CMake target dependencies
sections.text:
Each GT32U2086 application is a CMake project. The SDK's
`neon-mdf/CMakeLists.txt` is added as a subdirectory; do not build the SDK directory
as a standalone project.

```text
<app>
 ├── neon_mdf_driver
 │    ├── neon_mdf_device_GT32U2086
 │    └── neon_mdf_kconfig
 ├── neon_mdf_device_GT32U2086 + gcc (word-only runtime before libgcc)
 └── freertos_kernel (optional)
      ├── freertos_kernel_include → freertos_config → device
      ├── freertos_kernel_port_headers
      └── freertos_kernel_port (OBJECT, GCC_ARM_CM0)
```

| Target | Provides |
|---|---|
| `neon_mdf_device_GT32U2086` | SystemInit, startup, runtime, CMSIS/device includes, GT32U2086 macro and compiler policy |
| `neon_mdf_kconfig` | Include directory containing `sdkconfig.h` |
| `neon_mdf_driver` | Peripheral drivers and console when UART is enabled |
| `freertos_config` | Application-owned kernel configuration, linked to the device to inherit its policy |
| `freertos_kernel` | Kernel, heap_4 and Cortex-M0 port |

`neon_mdf_add_executable()` attaches the linker script and post-build image tool
to the application. The linker map corresponds to the ELF; `_image.bin` is the
BootROM binary. Programming, monitoring and menuconfig are host custom targets,
not firmware libraries.

See [BuildSystem](BuildSystem.md) for the configure/build flow and
[Architecture](Architecture.md) for the boundaries between SDK layers.

sections.heading: NEON-MDF architecture
sections.text:
NEON-MDF targets GT32U2086. Each application owns its CMake project and
configuration; the SDK provides device support, drivers, a console,
configuration tools and firmware packaging.

sections.heading: Layers
sections.text:
```text
Application (Src/, Inc/, Kconfig, sdkconfig)
        ↓
HAL drivers + console       FreeRTOS (optional)
        ↓                         ↓
GT32U2086 device: CMSIS, startup, SystemInit, word-only runtime
        ↓
GT32U2086 / BootROM v5
```

| Directory | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `neon-mdf/mcu-description/devices/GT32U2086.yaml` | Memory map, registers, IRQs and profiles |
| `neon-mdf/mcu-description/tools/` | Loader/model and Cortex-M0 code generation backend |
| `neon-mdf/arch/CortexM/CMSIS/Device/GT32U2086/` | Handwritten system/runtime code and generated reference snapshots |
| `<application>/build/GT32U2086/generated/GT32U2086/` | Build-local device headers, startup, linker, SVD and image metadata |
| `neon-mdf/arch/CortexM/CMSIS/CMSIS_5/` | CMSIS-Core, restricted to Cortex-M0 core and compiler headers |
| `neon-mdf/components/driver/` | Public APIs and GT32U2086 peripheral backends |
| `neon-mdf/components/console/` | `printf` formatter, `_write` and UART connection |
| `neon-mdf/rtos/` | FreeRTOS kernel, GCC Cortex-M0 port and heap_4 |
| `neon-mdf/cmake/` | Toolchain, device target, Kconfig and image/programming helpers |
| `neon-mdf/tools/` | CLI, image/UART tools and application templates |
| `examples/` | Independent firmware projects |
| `vscode-extension/` | Build/UART programming/monitor UI |

sections.heading: One device description
sections.text:
CMake runs `generate.py` during configuration. The YAML description generates
`GT32U2086.h`, the `mcu_device.h` alias, linker script, startup vectors, SVD and
an image CMake fragment. Generated files carry a banner; edit the YAML or
generator instead of their output. `system_GT32U2086.c/.h` and
`gt32u2086_runtime.c` are handwritten.

`profile_param` selects internal Flash (`normal`) or QSPI XIP (`xip`). The
physical memory map stays fixed; profiles define the header, IRQ relay and
application memory ranges. Each build directory owns its generated device
files, allowing concurrent normal/XIP builds in separate directories. See [Device YAML](DeviceYAML.md).

sections.heading: Drivers and runtime
sections.text:
Public headers are in `driver/<peripheral>/neon_<peripheral>.h`; backends are
in `driver/<peripheral>/platform/gt32u2086/`. `neon_mdf_driver` collects the
sources and propagates include paths, the device macro, compiler flags and
configuration to the application.

GT32U2086 SRAM requires word access. The device target propagates compiler
flags and provides word-only memory routines; applications, drivers and
FreeRTOS must share this policy. Access MMIO through driver APIs using the
required register widths.

sections.heading: Startup and images
sections.text:
For internal Flash, application vectors are linked at `0x00020080`. The image
tool places a 128-byte header at `0x00020000`. BootROM verifies the image and
hands off to the application, forwarding exceptions through the IRQ relay
because Cortex-M0 has no VTOR.

The SDK currently builds an application and its BootROM image. See
[GT32U2086](GT32U2086.md) and [Boot modes](GT32U2086BootModes.md) for the full contract.

sections.heading: GT32U2086 board and clock configuration
sections.text:
The compiler target and preset are `GT32U2086`. FU2 is an older product name,
not a CMake preset or CLI target. The BootROM signing domain `FU2-IMAGE-V1`
is a fixed protocol constant and must retain its spelling.

sections.heading: Select the actual clock
sections.text:
GT32U2086 is rated up to 60 MHz. FPGA peripheral examples normally describe a
10 MHz bitstream; assigning a software frequency does not change its clock.
An incorrect `SystemCoreClock` affects UART baud, SPI/QSPI rates, timer periods
and the FreeRTOS tick.

| Application | Clock setting |
|---|---|
| Peripheral examples | `CONFIG_GT32U2086_EXAMPLE_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ` in menuconfig/sdkconfig |
| `Printf_Log` | CMake `NEON_PRINTF_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ`, default `10000000` |
| New bare-metal/FreeRTOS template | CMake `NEON_APP_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ`, default `0` |

`0` selects CRM clock detection in `SystemCoreClockUpdate()`. For a template
application on a known 10 MHz FPGA, run from the app directory:

```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086 -DNEON_APP_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ=10000000
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

Existing `Blinky`/`FreeRTOS_Blinky` use the CRM policy unless the device target
receives `GT32U2086_FPGA_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ`. A hand-written application can add
this after including `tools/cmake/project.cmake` for a fixed board clock:

```cmake
target_compile_definitions(${NEON_MDF_DEVICE_TARGET} PUBLIC
  GT32U2086_FPGA_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ=10000000UL)
```

Use the actual measured/configured frequency. Verify UART bit timing, a TIM/PWM
period and the FreeRTOS tick on the board after changing its bitstream.

sections.heading: Pins and connected devices
sections.text:
Default driver `AUTO` routes refer to package pins and do not establish
FPGA/PMOD connector wiring. Record board revision, bitstream, connector,
voltage, pin mux and attached device before running a peripheral test.

| Function | SDK default |
|---|---|
| UART0 console | TX package 50, RX package 51; 19200 baud, 8N1 |
| GPIO input/output | PB5 button to GND with pull-up; PB7 output |
| SPI0/W5500 | SCK=60, MISO=61, MOSI=62, SS0=63; verify PMOD mapping |
| I2C0 | SDA=18, SCL=19; external pull-ups required |
| QSPI | SCK=68, CS0=72, IO0=71, IO1=70, IO2=69, IO3=64 |

Use the example README and board schematic together. `KEEP` leaves routing to
board code; release an `AUTO` route before another driver takes ownership.
Boot values `100`, `000`, `101` and `111` are logical SoC values, not physical
switch positions; see [boot modes](GT32U2086BootModes.md).

sections.heading: Storage reservations
sections.text:
`Flash_Read_Write` reserves internal sector `0x0009FE00..0x0009FFFF`.
The two QSPI NOR tests default to external offsets `0x0003C000..0x0003CFFF`.
Reserve these regions before destructive tests. QSPI test applications require
the normal profile and execute from internal Flash; mapped reads are separate
from booting firmware directly from QSPI.

sections.heading: GT32U2086 build system
sections.text:
Run CMake from the application directory. `CMakePresets.json` selects Ninja,
Arm GNU Toolchain, `NEON_MDF_TARGET=GT32U2086` and `build/GT32U2086` as the output directory.

sections.heading: Configuration
sections.text:
1. `project(<name> C ASM)` initializes the project with the preset's toolchain.
2. `tools/cmake/project.cmake` locates the SDK, validates the target and adds the SDK with `add_subdirectory`.
3. `cmake/mcu_variants.cmake` runs the generator for the `normal` or `xip` profile and creates the device library.
4. `cmake/kconfig.cmake` combines SDK/application Kconfig and generates `sdkconfig.h`/`.cmake`.
5. Drivers and console add sources according to configuration. The application registers its executable and optionally FreeRTOS.

Python reads the YAML; CMake receives the memory layout through
`build/GT32U2086/generated/GT32U2086/GT32U2086_image.cmake`. YAML and generator
changes trigger CMake configuration automatically. CMake uses `Python3_EXECUTABLE` for device generation, Kconfig and
packaging; select the `.venv` interpreter as described in [Setup](Setup.md).

sections.heading: Building and linking
sections.text:
`neon_mdf_add_executable()` links the application with the driver, device and
libgcc, and selects the generated linker script. `-u,__clzsi2` selects the
word-only runtime before libgcc helpers; `-nostdlib` keeps runtime and entry
point selection under SDK control.

After linking, `cmake/gt32u2086_image.cmake` runs objcopy, reports size and
invokes `tools/gt32u2086_image.py`. The tool validates ELF placement and packages
the header/payload.

| Artifact | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `<app>` | ELF with symbols for analysis/debugging |
| `<app>.map` | Linker map and memory ranges |
| `<app>.bin` | Payload starting at the vector base |
| `<app>_image.bin` | BootROM header + payload for internal Flash programming |

XIP profiles add `_xip` to binary names; see [GT32U2086](GT32U2086.md).

sections.heading: Common operation targets
sections.text:
```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target menuconfig
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target flash_uart_gt32u2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target serial_monitor
```

Programming/monitoring read `NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT`, baud and UART parameters at
**execution time**. Port/baud changes do not require reconfiguration. Programming
targets depend on the application so firmware is packaged before transmission.
For projects with multiple executables, use `<app>_flash_uart_gt32u2086` to select
the image; `flash_uart_gt32u2086` uses the first packaged executable.

sections.heading: Application configuration
sections.text:
`CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_*` controls optional drivers. GPIO, Flash, CRM and SYSCSR
are always-built infrastructure. UART also enables the console; applications
calling `printf` must enable UART. Each project owns its `sdkconfig`. See
[menuconfig](MenuConfig.md).

FreeRTOS is added explicitly with `neon_mdf_add_freertos()`, using the kernel,
GCC ARM_CM0 and heap_4. Other ports have been removed from the vendor subset.
See [FreeRTOS](FreeRTOSPort.md).

sections.heading: Start from a fresh configuration
sections.text:
```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086 --fresh
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

Use `--fresh` after changing the toolchain, Python or checkout path. The new
preset uses `build/GT32U2086`; old binaries are not outputs of the current source.
Each build directory owns its generated headers, startup, linker script, SVD
and image fragment under `generated/GT32U2086/`. Separate normal/XIP build
directories may run concurrently; do not run two configurations in one directory.
For example, configure XIP with `cmake --preset GT32U2086 -B build/GT32U2086-xip -DNEON_MDF_PROFILE=xip`,
then build with `cmake --build build/GT32U2086-xip`.
Changes to `sdkconfig`, sourced Kconfig files and device YAML are tracked by CMake.
CLI and direct builds regenerate configuration before compiling.
See [automated validation](HardwareValidation.md#automated-checks).

sections.heading: Testing and debugging GT32U2086
sections.text:
The current workflow is **build → program through UART → inspect UART output and
hardware measurements**. `neon-mdf/cmake/openocd/GT32U2086_openocd.cfg` remains a
placeholder; the SDK does not provide a complete JTAG/OpenOCD configuration for
programming or debugging GT32U2086.

sections.heading: Validate before running
sections.text:
```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
python ../../neon-mdf/tools/gt32u2086_image.py info build/GT32U2086/printf_log_image.bin
```

These commands use `Printf_Log`; substitute the image filename for other
applications. Check the normal image base `0x00020000`, 128-byte header and
application vector base `0x00020080`. Inspect the linker map for incorrect
Flash/RAM placement. `gt32u2086_flash.py --check-only` validates images without
opening a UART port; see [UART programming](GT32U2086Flashing.md).

sections.heading: Logs and measurements
sections.text:
Open the monitor at the application baud (19200, 8N1 by default). If no logs
appear, check the actual clock, UART mux, TX/RX/GND, baud and
`CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART=y`. Examples with the `fpga:>>` terminal typically
wait for `r` before running. Use a logic analyzer/oscilloscope to measure GPIO,
UART, SPI, I2C and PWM timing.

BootROM hands off with global interrupts masked. If polling works but ISRs do
not run, check peripheral configuration, NVIC and `__enable_irq()` in bare-metal
applications. See the IRQ relay mechanism in [GT32U2086](GT32U2086.md).

sections.heading: Preparing JTAG integration
sections.text:
Identify the adapter, JTAG transport, target script, Flash programming algorithm
and board reset behavior before replacing the placeholder and validating a
GDB/OpenOCD session. The extension can start an attach session from a
board-specific Cortex-Debug configuration. See [VS Code](VSCode.md#debug) for
the configuration and workflow.

BootROM firmware requires a header outside the raw ELF payload. When implementing
a debugger workflow, keep the header and code consistent: verify that the probe's
erase/program operations preserve the complete image. See the
[image format](GT32U2086.md).

sections.heading: GT32U2086 device description in YAML
sections.text:
The device description is in `neon-mdf/mcu-description/devices/GT32U2086.yaml`.
The loader validates it and the backend generates CMSIS headers, linker scripts,
startup code, SVD and an image CMake fragment. Reference schemas are in
`mcu-description/schema/`; executable validation is implemented in
`tools/mcu_desc/loader.py` and `memory_layout.py`.

sections.heading: Device and CPU information
sections.text:
```yaml
device: GT32U2086
vendor: FPTTelecom
family: GT32U2086
arch: cortex-m0
cpu:
  core: cortex-m0
  revision: r0p0
  max_freq_hz: 60000000
  nvic_priority_bits: 2
  num_irq: 32
  vtor_supported: false
```

`device`, `family` and `arch` identify the supported target. `max_freq_hz`
describes the CPU limit; it does not configure the board clock. Handwritten
system code determines the runtime clock. Other CPU fields control CMSIS macros
and vector generation.

sections.heading: Memory map and profiles
sections.text:
`memory` lists physical regions with `name`, `kind` (`flash`, `ram`, `rom`),
`address` and `size`. To relocate an image, use `profile_param` to select regions
and allocate application ranges rather than changing physical addresses.

Each `normal`/`xip` profile has `flash` and `ram` mappings containing `region`
and `layout`. Layout entries have `name`, `offset`, `size`, `usage` and an
optional description. Offsets are relative to the parent region;
`size: remaining` uses the rest of the region from that offset. Entries must fit
within the parent without overlap. Each mapping needs an `application` entry
with `usage: allocatable`.

| Profile | Image base | Vector base | Application RAM |
|---|---|---|---|
| `normal` | `0x00020000` | `0x00020080` | `0x01001000` to `0x0101FFFF` |
| `xip` | `0x30000000` | `0x30000080` | Same as normal |

`image_header` in Flash and `irq_relay` in SRAM are ROM reservations. GT32U2086
profiles reserve a 128-byte header and the first 4 KB of SRAM. Startup copies
and clears only application data/bss; the relay must remain intact. See
[GT32U2086](GT32U2086.md).

sections.heading: Peripherals and registers
sections.text:
Each peripheral has `name`, `base`, `registers`, and optionally `type` and a
description. Registers declare `name`, `offset`, `size`, `access`, reset values,
and optional `fields`/`aliases`. Access permissions are `ro`, `wo` or `rw`.

```yaml
registers:
  - name: CTRL
    offset: 0x00
    size: 32
    access: rw
    reset: 0x00000000
    fields:
      - {name: ENABLE, bit_offset: 0, bit_width: 1}
```

This illustrates syntax; actual addresses/bits must come from the device YAML
and hardware documentation. `aliases` describe multiple views of one address,
such as mode-dependent UART registers. Instances sharing a `type` must have
compatible register layouts. Generated headers use structs, reserved ranges and
bitfield macros derived from this data.

sections.heading: Interrupts
sections.text:
`interrupts` entries contain `number`, `name` and `description`. `number` is the
NVIC IRQ index from 0 to `cpu.num_irq - 1`; names generate `*_IRQn` and
`*_IRQHandler`. Entries are placed at **16 + number**, regardless of declaration
order. Undeclared IRQ slots are reserved. The loader rejects duplicate or
out-of-range IRQ numbers.

sections.heading: Regenerate and verify
sections.text:
From the repository root:

```sh
python neon-mdf/mcu-description/tools/generate.py --device GT32U2086 --profile normal
```

Then configure/build an application to check headers, vectors, layout and image:

```sh
cd examples/Printf_Log
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

CMake writes outputs under each build directory’s `generated/GT32U2086/`.
The manual command defaults to `build/generated/GT32U2086/normal` below the
current directory; use `--output-dir /path/to/output` to override it.
Use separate build directories for concurrent profiles. See [build system](BuildSystem.md).

sections.heading: GT32U2086 driver development
sections.text:
Drivers expose public APIs in
`components/driver/<peripheral>/neon_<peripheral>.h` with implementations in
`platform/gt32u2086/neon_<peripheral>.c`. All sources are collected in the
`neon_mdf_driver` CMake target.

sections.heading: Add or update a module
sections.text:
1. Compare bases, offsets, access permissions and bitfields in `GT32U2086.yaml`
   against hardware documentation. Update the YAML and regenerate when register data changes.
2. Define configuration/handle types and APIs in the public header, following the
   [coding convention](NEON_Coding_Convention_V1.3.md).
3. Implement the GT32U2086 backend: clock/reset, PAD mux, MMIO, errors and timeouts.
4. Add sources to the peripheral's CMake file; optional modules have Kconfig switches.
5. Add or update an application example to verify the changed behavior on hardware.

sections.heading: CMake and configuration integration
sections.text:
GPIO, Flash, CRM and SYSCSR are always-built infrastructure. Other peripherals
are controlled by `CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_*` in `components/driver/Kconfig`.
UART also enables the console. Example conditional source registration:

```cmake
if(CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART)
  target_sources(neon_mdf_driver PRIVATE
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_LIST_DIR}/platform/gt32u2086/neon_uart.c)
endif()
```

Some peripheral CMakeLists also use
`components/cmake/driver_helpers.cmake` to select the GT32U2086 backend. When
adding a module, register its subdirectory in `components/driver/CMakeLists.txt`
and update `neon_config.h` if the public header needs a module guard. See
[menuconfig](MenuConfig.md).

sections.heading: Hardware rules
sections.text:
- Use aligned 32-bit word accesses for SRAM; buffers must own every word accessed by the runtime.
- Follow register widths and ordering for MMIO; do not use memory routines on registers.
- Save and restore PRIMASK in critical sections; do not unconditionally enable interrupts on exit.
- `timeout_polls` counts polling iterations, not milliseconds.
- Calculate timing from actual clocks; do not assume maximum CPU frequency.
- Initialize clocks and PAD mux before enabling peripherals; handle W1C/RO/WO status correctly.

sections.heading: Verification
sections.text:
Build the module's example with appropriate enabled/disabled configurations.
Inspect images/maps after runtime or memory-layout changes. Use a board to verify
IRQs, clocks, FIFOs, DMA and error/timeout behavior; a successful build does not
verify physical timing.

[GPIO_Input_Output](../examples/GPIO_Input_Output/README.md),
[UART_RX_Interrupt](../examples/UART_RX_Interrupt/README.md) and
[SPI_DMA](../examples/SPI_DMA/README.md) provide starting points for driver verification.

sections.heading: Your first GT32U2086 application
sections.text:
Complete [environment setup](Setup.md) and activate `.venv` before starting.
The quickest approach is to create a project from a template or copy a suitable example.

sections.heading: Create from VS Code
sections.text:
Open the repository or an existing example and run **NEON-MDF: Create New App...**.
Name the project, select bare-metal or FreeRTOS, and choose its destination.
The wizard copies the SDK template and writes the application name and the
relative SDK path. See [VS Code](VSCode.md) for installation and SDK selection.

sections.heading: Create from a terminal
sections.text:
Run the following cross-platform script from the repository root using Python
in `.venv`. It creates `examples/MyApp` from the bare-metal template:

```python
from pathlib import Path
import shutil

source = Path("neon-mdf/tools/templates")
destination = Path("examples/MyApp")
shutil.copytree(source, destination)
for path in destination.rglob("*"):
    if path.is_file():
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        text = text.replace("__APP_NAME__", "MyApp")
        text = text.replace("__NEON_MDF_RELATIVE_PATH__", "../../neon-mdf")
        path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
```

Save this as a temporary script and run it with `python`, or execute it in the
Python REPL. `copytree` reports an error if the destination already exists.
For a FreeRTOS application, replace `templates` with `templates_freertos`;
kernel configuration is in `Inc/FreeRTOSConfig.h`. For applications outside the
repository, replace `../../neon-mdf` with the SDK path relative to your project.

sections.heading: Project structure
sections.text:
```text
MyApp/
├── CMakeLists.txt       # Application name, SDK path and source list
├── CMakePresets.json    # GT32U2086 preset, Arm GNU, Ninja, build/GT32U2086
├── Kconfig             # Optional application-specific settings
├── Src/main.c          # Application entry point
└── Inc/FreeRTOSConfig.h # FreeRTOS template only
```

After the first configuration, `sdkconfig` stores application settings and
`build/` contains generated artifacts. Keep `sdkconfig` in version control;
do not commit `build/`.

The application calls `project()` before including the SDK:

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(MyApp C ASM)
include($ENV{NEON_MDF_PATH}/tools/cmake/project.cmake)
neon_mdf_add_executable(MyApp Src/main.c)
```

This minimal version requires `NEON_MDF_PATH`; templates already provide
SDK path discovery. Add `.c` files to `neon_mdf_add_executable()` and register
include directories with `target_include_directories(MyApp PRIVATE Inc)` as needed.

sections.heading: Configure and build
sections.text:
```sh
cd examples/MyApp
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

For a known 10 MHz FPGA, configure the template with
`cmake --preset GT32U2086 -DNEON_APP_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ=10000000`. The default `0`
uses CRM clock detection. See [board configuration](BoardConfiguration.md).

The template enables UART through the default driver configuration. Check
`CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART=y` in `sdkconfig` if the application calls `printf`.
The main output is `build/GT32U2086/MyApp_image.bin`; a `.bin` without `_image`
is the payload without its header. `MyApp` is the ELF and `MyApp.map` is the linker map.

sections.heading: Program, run and edit
sections.text:
```sh
cmake -E env NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 NEON_MDF_SERIAL_BAUD=19200 cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target flash_uart_gt32u2086
cmake -E env NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 NEON_MDF_MONITOR_BAUD=19200 cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target serial_monitor
```

Set the port and baud for your board. Select boot mode `100`, wait for the loader
to be ready, then press RESET. The template prints `MyApp is running` through
UART0. If initial logs are missed, keep the monitor open and reset in boot mode
`000`. See [UART programming](GT32U2086Flashing.md).

Edit `Src/main.c`, build and program again. For a bare-metal application using
interrupts, finish peripheral/NVIC configuration before calling `__enable_irq()`;
BootROM hands off with global interrupts masked. The FreeRTOS port enables
interrupts when starting the scheduler; see [FreeRTOS](FreeRTOSPort.md).

sections.heading: Configuration and CLI
sections.text:
```sh
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target menuconfig
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

The CLI provides a shorter way to invoke the same CMake targets. From the
application directory, after setting `NEON_MDF_PATH`:

```sh
python "$NEON_MDF_PATH/tools/neon_mdf.py" -p /dev/ttyUSB0 -b 19200 build flash-uart-gt32u2086 monitor
```

Available actions are `build`, `flash-uart-gt32u2086`, `monitor`, `menuconfig`
and `set-target`. `GT32U2086` is the only target; see `--help` for parameters.

Check the SDK version from any directory after setting `NEON_MDF_PATH`:

```sh
python "$NEON_MDF_PATH/tools/neon_mdf.py" --version
```

sections.heading: FreeRTOS on GT32U2086
sections.text:
The SDK integrates FreeRTOS-Kernel with the **`GCC_ARM_CM0` port** and **`heap_4`**.
Each application owns its `Inc/FreeRTOSConfig.h`; the integration helper is
`neon-mdf/cmake/freertos.cmake`.

sections.heading: CMake integration
sections.text:
After including `tools/cmake/project.cmake`:

```cmake
include(${NEON_MDF_PATH}/cmake/freertos.cmake)
neon_mdf_add_freertos(${NEON_MDF_TARGET} ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/Inc)
neon_mdf_add_executable(my_app Src/main.c)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE freertos_kernel)
```

The helper creates `freertos_config`, adds the application configuration include
path and links the device target so the kernel/port inherit its word-only SRAM
policy. Cortex-M0 flags are applied to both kernel and port. Preserve this
integration when adding applications.

The vendored kernel contains word-only patches for byte fields, task names,
memory access and static-object ABI layout. Preserve these when updating
upstream and rebuild application/kernel objects together.

sections.heading: Clock, heap and stack
sections.text:
`configCPU_CLOCK_HZ` uses `SystemCoreClock`; the clock must match the hardware.
FPGA peripheral examples typically set
`CONFIG_GT32U2086_EXAMPLE_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ=10000000`.
`configMINIMAL_STACK_SIZE` and stack sizes passed to `xTaskCreate` are measured
in **words**, whereas `configTOTAL_HEAP_SIZE` is in **bytes**. Check the linker
map and actual stack usage before increasing task/queue counts.
New templates accept `-DNEON_APP_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ=10000000` for a known 10 MHz
FPGA; the default `0` uses CRM clock detection. See [board configuration](BoardConfiguration.md).

sections.heading: Exception handlers and BootROM
sections.text:
GT32U2086 uses Cortex-M0 without VTOR. BootROM v5 forwards exceptions to the
application vectors through the SRAM IRQ relay. Startup must preserve this
relay; do not substitute linker scripts or startup code that bypass the device profile.

Set `configCHECK_HANDLER_INSTALLATION=0`: the port's VTOR-based vector check is
incompatible with the BootROM relay. Cortex-M0 has no CLZ instruction, so keep
`configUSE_PORT_OPTIMISED_TASK_SELECTION=0`. Set `configENABLE_MPU=0`.
The port provides SVC/PendSV/SysTick handlers using the names expected by startup.

BootROM hands off with `PRIMASK=1`. The FreeRTOS port enables interrupts when
starting the scheduler. Before scheduler startup, only enable interrupts once
handlers and interrupt sources are ready.

sections.heading: Data and console
sections.text:
GT32U2086 requires aligned 32-bit SRAM word access. The kernel uses the device
target's word-only memory runtime. Queue items should have sizes that are
multiples of four and own every accessed word. Do not pass pointers to local
buffers between tasks after their lifetime has ended.

The console does not automatically serialize concurrent task output. Use a
single logging task or protect sequences of console operations with a mutex
when multiple producers are present.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.text:
- [FreeRTOS_Blinky](../examples/FreeRTOS_Blinky/): two tasks toggle GPIO at different periods.
- [FreeRTOS_Peripheral_Queue](../examples/FreeRTOS_Peripheral_Queue/README.md):
  transfers peripheral events through a queue, with a UART terminal to run the example.
- `neon-mdf/tools/templates_freertos/`: a single-task template for new applications.

Successful builds/links verify kernel integration. Board execution is needed
to verify interrupts, tick timing, preemption, response time and stack/heap margins.

sections.heading: GT32U2086 build and boot contract
sections.text:
The target name, device macro and build preset are `GT32U2086`. All GT32U2086 applications
use the RTL BootROM v5 image contract from Test_VP; there is no separate ROM
variant or legacy raw-slot build. Peripheral addresses follow GT32U2086's current
register map. ROM revision and MCU register-map revision are separate concepts.
The Cortex-M0 core supports up to 60 MHz. A fixed FPGA clock setting describes
the clock actually supplied by the board, rather than the maximum CPU rating.

| Resource | Normal Flash | QSPI XIP |
|---|---|---|
| Complete boot image base | `0x00020000` | `0x30000000` |
| Header size | `0x80` | `0x80` |
| Application vector base | `0x00020080` | `0x30000080` |
| Payload capacity | `0x7FF80` | `0x3FF80` |
| Application RAM | `0x01001000`–`0x0101FFFF` | Same |
| Initial stack top | `0x01020000` | Same |

Physical Flash/RAM definitions remain unchanged in `GT32U2086.yaml`; its normal/XIP
profiles reserve the image header and the first 4 KB of SRAM. The first two SRAM
words hold the ROM-published vector base and exclusive payload end. Startup
copies only application `.data` and clears only application `.bss`, preserving
those words. Cortex-M0 has no VTOR: interrupt forwarding is provided by the ROM.

BootROM v5 hands over with `PRIMASK=1`, all NVIC sources disabled and pending
interrupts cleared. An application using interrupts must call `__enable_irq()`
after its runtime and interrupt sources are ready; `NVIC_EnableIRQ()` alone
does not clear the global mask. Peripheral drivers preserve PRIMASK across
their critical sections.

sections.heading: Build
sections.text:
For Test_VP or a Neon application such as Blinky:

```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086 --fresh
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

The linker script is generated inside each build directory from the selected `GT32U2086.yaml` profile.
`neon_mdf_add_executable()` packages the ROM image
automatically. Standalone examples call `neon_mdf_add_gt32u2086_image()` from
`neon-mdf/cmake/gt32u2086_image.cmake` after generating the GT32U2086 device files.

Outputs:

| File | Profile `normal` | Profile `xip` |
|---|---|---|
| Raw vector/code/data payload | `<app>.bin` | `<app>_xip.bin` |
| Header plus payload for ROM boot | `<app>_image.bin` | `<app>_image_xip.bin` |

An ELF suffix, when configured by the project, also appears in the raw payload
filename, before `_xip` when present. ELF and target names keep their existing names.
The default app version is `0.0.1`; set `-DNEON_MDF_GT32U2086_APP_VERSION=1.2.3` to change
it. Builds produce non-secure images with header and payload CRCs. Signing and
NVR generation are available through the shared tool:

```sh
python3 neon-mdf/tools/gt32u2086_image.py info /path/to/app_image.bin
python3 neon-mdf/tools/gt32u2086_image.py nvr --secure-mode 0 -o /path/to/nvr.bin
python3 neon-mdf/tools/gt32u2086_image.py image --input /path/to/app.bin \
  --elf /path/to/app --flash-addr 0x20000 --key /path/to/key.pem \
  --output /path/to/app_image.bin
```

Non-secure packing uses Python's standard library; signing needs `cryptography`.
Image packing checks the ELF vector location, SRAM placement, stack, reset
address and Flash capacity, rejecting stale raw-image layouts.

sections.heading: XIP
sections.text:
Keep the target/preset name `GT32U2086` and select the memory profile:

```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086 --fresh -DNEON_MDF_PROFILE=xip
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

Project helpers keep generated device files under each build directory.
For concurrent normal/XIP builds, use a separate directory such as
`cmake --preset GT32U2086 -B build/GT32U2086-xip -DNEON_MDF_PROFILE=xip`,
then `cmake --build build/GT32U2086-xip`. An image header's Flash base must match its linked
payload. QSPI-copy boot uses an internal-Flash-linked image; it is distinct from
an XIP image linked at `0x30000080`.

sections.heading: UART programming
sections.text:
GT32U2086 Flash Tool 1.0 is integrated with the image-packaging helper. Configure
without serial settings, then pass the port and ROMCODE baud at execution time:

```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake -E env NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 NEON_MDF_SERIAL_BAUD=19200 \
  cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target flash_uart_gt32u2086
```

Select hardware boot mode `100`, wait for `[WAIT] UART is ready`, then press
RESET. This target programs the normal image into Internal Flash. XIP images
are rejected before UART is opened. See [flash firmware GT32U2086 via UART](GT32U2086Flashing.md)
for boot modes, runtime parameters, monitoring and troubleshooting.
For per-mode firmware preparation and boot procedures, see
[GT32U2086 boot modes and firmware workflow](GT32U2086BootModes.md).

sections.heading: Runtime and peripherals
sections.text:
GT32U2086 application SRAM data accesses are aligned 32-bit transactions. The SDK
propagates the compiler policy and supplies word-access memory helpers.
The GT32U2086 FreeRTOS port widens internal byte flags/locks and uses aligned-word
access for task names and SVC decoding; static object layouts follow the same
ABI. Rebuild all objects when changing targets. Custom sources and third-party
libraries must obey the same bus contract.

Include `<string.h>` to use the GT32U2086 runtime implementations of `memcpy`,
`memmove`, `memset`, `memcmp`, `memchr`, `strlen`, `strcmp`, `strncmp`,
`strcpy`, `strncpy`, `strcat`, `strncat`, `strchr`, `strrchr`, `strstr`,
`strspn`, `strcspn` and `strpbrk`. Standard GT32U2086 project helpers link these
implementations automatically; they access bytes through aligned 32-bit words.
Each buffer/string must own the complete aligned words containing its bytes,
including its terminator. For example, use `uint32_t storage[16]` as a 64-byte
buffer and pass `(char *)storage`. Destination capacity and C string rules
still apply: `strncpy` pads to its count and may omit the terminator when
truncated; `strncat` needs space for the existing string, appended bytes and
terminator. These functions do not support MMIO or concurrently modified DMA
buffers, and do not change direct byte/halfword accesses in application code.

Drivers, console, applications and the FreeRTOS port use these standard
`<string.h>` functions for normal-memory buffers. Their implementations are
linked from `gt32u2086_runtime.c`; only that file uses `neon_utils_memory.h` as its internal
backend. Peripheral registers still use explicit
volatile word accesses: read a register into a `uint32_t` local, then use
`memcpy` to publish its bytes to a RAM buffer. Do not pass MMIO addresses
directly to the memory/string functions.

GT32U2086 builds `printf` and its `_write` output hook when
`CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART=y`; no separate printf feature flag is needed.
Disabling UART removes both the UART backend and console from the build.
Include `<stdio.h>` and call `printf`: the `_write` output hook initializes
UART0 at 19200 baud, 8N1 on first output, using `SystemCoreClock`. Attaching an
initialized UART through `neon_console_attach_uart()` is optional when a different
UART/baud is needed. The word-only formatter supports strings and integer/hex
formats, including 64-bit integers; floating point and full newlib stdio are
not supported. See [PrintfLogging.md](PrintfLogging.md) and
[Printf_Log](../examples/Printf_Log/README.md). Standard GT32U2086 project helpers
select the SDK's word-only CLZ runtime before libgcc, including when normal
clock calculations require 64-bit division.

UART polling follows `dti_usart_ctrl_ug_rev1p3`: TX waits for LSR[5] THRF=0
before each THR write and returns when all bytes are queued, without waiting
for LSR[6] TEMT. Wait for TEMT separately before reset, baud changes or pin
changes; otherwise queued output can be lost. RX waits for LSR[0] DR=1.
Use `neon_uart_wait_tx_complete()` to wait for TEMT with a bounded polling
budget before reconfiguration. `neon_uart_try_receive()` reads one available
element into a complete aligned `uint32_t` without waiting, returns TIMEOUT
when empty, and may run in the UART ISR while polling TX is BUSY_TX. It keeps
the interrupted TX state intact. Use only one RX consumer and serialize
configuration/teardown; do not call polling receive concurrently with ISR RX.
FCR[0] is active-low: 0 enables FIFOs, 1 selects non-FIFO mode and clears
their counters. ClearRxFIFO/ClearTxFIFO require FIFO mode. This revision
does not define RX threshold bits, so GT32U2086 accepts only the default
`fifo_threshold` value and returns NOT_SUPPORTED for other selections.

IIR pending is active-high. IDs are 0=none, 1=TX full, 2=RX ready, 3=line
error, 4=character timeout, 5=DMA TX done and 6=DMA RX done. The old TX_READY
names are compatibility aliases for TX_FULL on GT32U2086. RX_TIMEOUT now has ID 4;
MODEM is a reserved logical ID outside the GT32U2086 hardware ID range. Rebuild
applications using the updated header. `NEON_UART_INTERRUPT_ALL` selects
sources only; AUTO_CLEAR and MANUAL_CLEAR select clearing policy separately.
enable AUTO_CLEAR clears IER[4]; enable MANUAL_CLEAR sets it. In manual mode,
read IIR once through GetInterruptID and check NONE, because reading IIR also
acknowledges the event. A separate IsInterruptPending call can consume it.

CLKS[0] is the clock-fault flag, [12:1] contains the failed APB address and
[13] the command (0=write, 1=read). The driver caches a fault in
`handle.clock_status` before the hardware clears CLKS on read; only the flag
sets `NEON_UART_ERROR_CLOCK`. The remaining fields are diagnostic metadata.
Nine-bit TX selects LCR_EXT[3]=1 so THR accepts the ninth data bit. Five-bit
data with the public two-stop-bit setting is rejected because this hardware
combination actually produces 1.5 stop bits. parity follows Table 14 of the
guide; the EPS prose in Table 13 contradicts that table and needs RTL/hardware
confirmation before changing parity polarity.

ADC and DMA APIs now describe the current hardware rather than the older IPs:

- ADC init uses `channel`, `sample_source`, `sample_count`, `sample_clock_low`,
  `sample_clock_high` and `setup_wait`; call `neon_adc_get_default_config()` first.
  `neon_adc_read_samples()` returns 12-bit samples in a `uint16_t` buffer owning
  its complete aligned words. It reads sample slots, not a byte FIFO.
- DMA uses native FTEL channel command registers. Config fields include
  `transfer_size`, `read_config`, `write_config`, `control` and `peripheral_config`.
  `StartChannel()` takes instance/config; `FireChannel()` takes instance/channel;
  `MemCpy()` takes instance/channel/destination/source/byte count/timeout. PL330 program
  buffers and debug instructions are removed. GT32U2086 requires aligned source and
  destination addresses, word-sized bursts and a byte count divisible by four,
  at most 1020 bytes per call. DMA timeout zero explicitly waits indefinitely.
- AES keeps the logical ECB/CBC/CTR API and uses native key/IV/input/output banks
  with READY/DONE polling. Serialize the singleton engine between tasks.
- The old OTP/eFuse driver is unavailable in the current memory map and is
  kept under `components/driver/efuse`, disabled in builds.
  ROM security records use Flash NVR via the Flash driver.

`neon_adc_read_samples()` and `neon_crc_calculate()` now take a final timeout
argument: a total poll budget, not milliseconds. Zero only checks readiness;
a timeout stops the ADC/CRC engine. `neon_dma_memcpy()` also takes a final poll
budget; a DMA wait timeout does not abort a channel already running.

SPI0 and SPI1 follow **DTI SPI User Guide rev1.1, chapter 9**. Offsets are:

| Register | Offset | Register | Offset |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| TX | `0x00` | CTRL | `0x04` |
| CONFCMD | `0x08` | DLR | `0x0C` |
| AR | `0x10` | ABR | `0x14` |
| FIFO | `0x18` | CLK | `0x1C` |
| CMDCONF | `0x20` | TREG0 | `0x24` |
| TREG1 | `0x28` | TREG2 | `0x2C` |
| RX | `0x30` | CLKS | `0x34` |
| STT | `0x38` | STT_DMA | `0x3C` |
| CTRL_RX | `0x40` | CTRL_TX | `0x44` |

CTRL uses SPI_MODE `[1:0]` (0=legacy slave, 1=legacy master, 2=extended DDR),
CPOL `[2]`, CPHA `[3]`, LSB `[4]`, INT_EN `[5]`, SS_MODE `[6]`, SS_FORCE `[7]`,
SS_LONG `[8]` and DMA_ENABLE `[9]`. Legacy master mode 3/MSB/polling is `0x0D`.
The old one-bit `SPI_CTRL_MA_EN` definition is replaced by `SPI_CTRL_SPI_MODE`.
Regenerate headers/SVD from GT32U2086.yaml and rebuild all affected objects.

Rev1.1 has conflicting legacy text: Table 4 lists RX at `0x1C`, while
section 4.3, Table 7 and section 9.14 consistently specify `0x30`. Section
7.1 mentions FIFO at `0x08`; sections 4.1/9.8 and Table 7 specify `0x18`.
One paragraph in 7.1 reverses TRAN_DONE polarity; Table 21 in 9.17 and the
subsequent rearm sequence use 1=complete. The HAL follows these register
descriptions and the consistent master/rearm sequences.

The SPI polling APIs implement legacy 8/16/24/32-bit master and 8-bit slave.
`neon_spi_set_data_width()` changes frame width while idle without resetting
the controller, preserving manual SS hold for header/payload sequences.
Extended DDR and circular-DMA registers are defined for inspection/raw use;
these modes are not implemented by the legacy transfer APIs.

GT32U2086 defaults to a pause of 10 complete SCK periods between data bytes,
including bytes within a 16/24/32-bit word. The default is defined by
`NEON_SPI_GT32U2086_B2B_SCK_CYCLES` under `#ifdef GT32U2086` in `spi/neon_spi.h`.
`timing.between_frames_unit=NEON_SPI_B2B_SCK_CYCLES` converts
`between_frames * 2 * (divider + 1)` to core-clock cycles in `TREG1.T_B2B`.
`neon_spi_set_clock_divider()` preserves the requested number of SCK
periods. Use `NEON_SPI_B2B_CORE_CYCLES` to program a raw core-cycle delay;
zero disables the byte pause. Initialization, timing changes and divider
changes reject values that cannot fit the 16-bit register before modifying
hardware. Rebuild all objects after the timing-structure change.

The `SPI_W5500` menu key `b` performs a read-only 10..0 SCK-period sweep.
It validates a 32-byte TX SRAM CRC32 reference at 10 periods, then compares
repeated reads against that fixed reference and checks VERSIONR=0x04.
It reports CRC/ID/transport errors and the smallest zero-error setting in
that run, restores the original SPI settings and leaves auto ping/pong off.
The sample count is `CONFIG_SPI_W5500_B2B_TRIES` (default 1000 per level).
This checks repeatability of inactive TX SRAM, not correctness against a
known written pattern; the reported minimum is specific to mode, speed and
sample count. An unstable reference or cancelled run reports no minimum.

There is no shifter-BUSY bit in rev1.1. After FIFO completion, master polling
adds a conservative core-cycle guard for the final serial clocks and applicable
SS setup/hold/timeout/inter-byte timing. It uses the existing polling budget,
assumes CPU and SPI core share the GT32U2086 system clock, and does not take over
SysTick or mask interrupts. Manual HOLD intentionally keeps CS asserted.
A polling timeout blocks further transfers/configuration until Init or DeInit
resets the controller, so a partial frame cannot silently contaminate a retry.

SPI DMA configuration is one-shot: program a disabled channel, pulse its CLEAR
bit `[21]`, then arm it. Reconfiguration requires the previous enabled channel
to report TRAN_DONE. Each direction is cleared separately; arming the other
direction for full duplex remains supported. Disable accepts a config with
only `state=DISABLE`. SS_FORCE alone can change during active DMA, as allowed
by section 4.4; SS_MODE/SS_LONG and other settings require idle hardware.
The application still configures DMAC and the DMA handshake/channel selection.

sections.heading: Automatic pin configuration
sections.text:
GT32U2086 UART, I2C, SPI, QSPI and PWM initialize their SYSCSR pad/mux routes by
default. GPIO already configures its own GPIO mux and supported pad properties.
Applications do not need to write SYSCSR in a peripheral example.

| Driver | Default package pins |
|---|---|
| UART0 | TX=50, RX=51 |
| UART1 | TX=58, RX=59 |
| UART2 | TX=12, RX=13; JTAG mux is released/restored automatically |
| UART3 | TX=24, RX=25 |
| UART4 | TX=26, RX=48 |
| I2C0 | SDA=18, SCL=19 |
| SPI0 | SCK=60, MISO=61, MOSI=62, SS0=63 |
| SPI1 | SCK=20, MISO=21, MOSI=22, SS0=23 |
| QSPI | SCK=68, SSN=72, D0=71, D1=70, D2=69, D3=64 |
| PWM0/PWM1 | 73/74 |
| PWM on TIM0 | PWM_T0=48 (PB6) |

The serial/PWM backends share a SYSCSR helper that configures input feedback,
high drive, open-source off, and push-pull (UART/SPI/QSPI/PWM) or open-drain
(I2C). It supports all 24 pad indexes per side; pull and slew settings are kept.
I2C requires external bus pull-ups. Mux and pad bits are saved on the first
initialization and restored by DeInit. Reinitializing an active route keeps
the original snapshot; unrelated pins and later changes to their bits survive.
PWM AUTO routes channel 0; channel 1 requires KEEP because no package route
is defined for it. Deinitializing a KEEP channel leaves the AUTO route intact.
Drivers sharing a physical pin must be used sequentially.

Use each driver's `NEON_<driver>_PIN_CONFIG_KEEP` option when the board already
manages pin setup; AUTO is the zero/default value. Deinitialize an AUTO route
before handing its pins to board code or another driver. SPI masters with
`SLAVE_SELECT_NONE` configure only SCK/MISO/MOSI, leaving external GPIO CS
alone. Slave mode also configures SS0. SS1..3 have no package mapping and
return `NEON_NOT_MAPPED` in AUTO; KEEP allows board-managed routing.
UART RTS/CTS also requires KEEP because no default package mapping is defined.

Call `neon_*_get_default_config()` or zero-initialize configuration structs;
QSPI now also provides `neon_qspi_get_default_config()`. SPI/PWM/QSPI configs
have a new `pin_config` field: rebuild all users of these headers. Timer APIs
used only as internal counters and other APIs without a mapped pin function
do not change SYSCSR pin routing.

UART enforces one initialized handle per instance. DeInit releases ownership;
initialization failures release it too. RTC years use all four BCD digits
(1..9999), with calendar validation in SetDate.

QSPI supports SDR mode 0/3, Single/Dual/Quad phases, 1..4-byte addresses,
alternate bytes and memory-mapped reads. Zero-initialize command structures;
zero address size retains the three-byte default. Rebuild all users after
the configuration and command structure changes.

For an indirect transfer, call `neon_qspi_send_command()`, then pump the FIFO
with `neon_qspi_transmit_words()` or `neon_qspi_receive_words()`, then call
`neon_qspi_wait_complete()`. Buffers contain aligned packed words, low serial
byte first, and must have room for `ceil(data_length / 4)` words. The driver
converts logical byte counts to `DLR = data_length - 1`, checks FIFO full/empty,
and requires TC plus an idle controller before reporting completion. Legacy
`neon_qspi_wait_ready()` also finishes a pending command; the hardware BUSY
bit alone does not prove completion. After a timeout, abort before starting
another command. A failed partial buffer transfer leaves data pending; abort
it rather than restarting the same buffer from its first word.

For example, read a three-byte JEDEC ID after successful initialization:

```c
neon_qspi_command_t command = {
    .instruction = 0x9FU,
    .instruction_lines = NEON_QSPI_LINES_1,
    .data_lines = NEON_QSPI_LINES_1,
    .data_length = 3U,
    .receive_enable = 1U,
};
uint32_t id = 0U; /* Wire bytes occupy bits 7:0, 15:8 and 23:16. */
neon_status_t status = neon_qspi_send_command(QSPI_APB, &command);
if (status == NEON_OK) {
    status = neon_qspi_receive_words(QSPI_APB, &id, 100000U);
}
if (status == NEON_OK) {
    status = neon_qspi_wait_complete(QSPI_APB, 100000U);
}
```

Command-only frames temporarily use at least divider /32 and observe their
start before returning, even without TC. The start wait is bounded by
`NEON_QSPI_COMMAND_START_TIMEOUT_POLLS`. Successful completion or abort restores the
selected divider. Controller completion does not indicate the end of a NOR
erase/program cycle: the application must still read the chip's status/WIP.

Configure the NOR protocol/QE first, then use
`neon_qspi_enable_memory_mapped()` and read aligned words from the QSPI_XIP
window. `neon_qspi_abort()` flushes FIFOs and returns to indirect mode before
reconfiguration or DeInit. The code, constants, and other bus masters must
not access QSPI memory while changing/aborting its configuration. Automatic
status-polling, DDR and DMA transfers are not implemented by these APIs.

On the current FPGA backend TIM status is read-only live event state:
`STT_CH0` is at offset `0x4C`, `STT_CH1` at `0x50`. Reading flags does not
clear them or acknowledge an IRQ. UPDATE drops when the counter leaves the
reload condition. `neon_tim_clear_flag()` and `neon_pwm_clear_flags()` return
`NEON_NOT_SUPPORTED`; do not write STT. The periodic example bounds its wait
for UPDATE to drop and disables its IRQ on expiry. Measure event duration and
IRQ behavior on the actual bitstream. PWM shares this register contract.

The optional WDT driver provides config/DeInit/Refresh, counter reads and
interrupt acknowledgment. config enables its CRM clock and starts the watchdog;
timeout_range is the raw TOP value, so choose it for the board's watchdog clock.

ADC/AES/DMA/CRC/RTC/TRNG require CRM clock/reset setup before access.
GPIO has ClockEnable; UART/I2C/SPI/QSPI/TIM/PWM/WDT manage their own clocks at config.
The Test_VP 10-MHz fixed FPGA clock remains specific to that example. ROM v5
compatibility does not change silicon clock configuration or assume every board
uses the same oscillator.

The optional `gt32u2086_bootrom` target builds the vendored RTL ROM sources; see
`neon-mdf/components/bootrom/README.md`. Deploy applications against the chip's
ROM or the reference VP runner's pinned ROM and corresponding NVR policy.

documents.title: Boot mode and firmware GT32U2086 running procedure

sections.heading: Boot mode and firmware GT32U2086 running procedure
Starting principle
sections.text:
After Reset or power, GT32U2086 runs ROMCODE first. ROMCODE reads `SYSCSR_STATUS[2:0]` to select firmware
source, check image and switch to application if conditions are valid. User sets boot mode by
pin/jumper/switch according to board design; PC-side software parameter does not manually see
changing these pins.

The code in the documentation is the logical value of the SoC, not the jumper number or switch order
on a specific board. Use the board diagram to determine how the logic levels are set, keeping the
configuration stable during Reset.

| `STATUS[2:0]` | `MODE[1:0]` | `BOOT` | Modes | Image source | Application Running Location |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `000` | `00` | `0` | Internal Flash | Image flashed in Internal Flash | Internal Flash |
| `100` | `10` | `0` | USART update | PC send image via UART | Internal Flash after update |
| `101` | `10` | `1` | QSPI indirect update | Image from external QSPI source | Internal Flash after copying |
| `111` | `11` | `1` | QSPI XIP | Image Flashed in External QSPI Flash | Direct from External QSPI Flash |

The codes `001`, `010`, `011`, `110` failed to select the application boot path. ROMCODE returned to
Reset processing and reread the status. For consistent operation, set a valid mode and then press
Reset.

sections.heading: Prepare the right image
sections.text:
The SDK packages the image in the following structure:

```text
[header 128 bytes][vector table of application][code/data of application]
```

| The contents | Profile `normal` | Profile `xip` |
|---|---|---|
| Used for mode | `000`, `100`, `101` | `111` |
| address image viewed from CPU | `0x00020000` | `0x30000000` |
| address vector table | `0x00020080` | `0x30000080` |
| maximum size, including headers | `0x80000` byte (512 KB) | `0x40000` bytes (256 KB XIP window) |
| File used to flash | `<app>_image.bin` | `<app>_image_xip.bin` |

The program's associated address must match the profile and header. Do not change the address in the
header of image `normal` to turn it into an XIP image.

Build default profile from application directory:

```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

If the project has previously selected XIP, switch back with:

```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086 --fresh -DNEON_MDF_PROFILE=normal
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

Build image XIP:

```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086 --fresh -DNEON_MDF_PROFILE=xip
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

Profile is the image parameter affecting linker and code should be selected in the configure step.
Port/baud is a communication parameter when flashing, only transmitted at the target flash run. The
generated device/linker files belong to the build directory. For concurrent normal/XIP
builds use separate directories, for example `-B build/GT32U2086-xip` for XIP.

Check the image before flashing, from the root repository:

```sh
python3 neon-mdf/tools/gt32u2086_flash.py \
  --image /path/to/my_app_image.bin --check-only
```

sections.heading: Mode 000 — Running from Internal Flash
sections.text:
1. Prepare image profile `normal` and flash to Internal Flash first, for example according to the USART
   update process in the next entry.
2. Select the boot code `000` on your board.
3. Press Reset or power it back on.
4. ROMCODE checks the existing image at `0x00020000`, including header, CRC, vector and requires
   authentication according to NVR policy. If valid, ROMCODE switches to the application.
5. Check the result of application: LED, UART or written peripheral function.

This mode does not wait for the PC to send firmware. Do not use the UART tool to request image
burning while the board is in `000` mode.

sections.heading: Mode 100 — flash via UART and run from Internal Flash
sections.text:
1. Build application according to `normal` profile. Board must have valid NVR policy, compatible with
   image Secure/Non-secure used.
2. Connect the UART flash correctly according to the board and select boot mode `100`. Close the other
   Serial Monitor holding the port.
3. From the application folder, run:

   ```sh
   cmake -E env \
     NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 \
     NEON_MDF_SERIAL_BAUD=19200 \
     NEON_MDF_UART_BYTE_GAP_MS=2 \
     NEON_MDF_UART_LOG=full \
     cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target flash_uart_gt32u2086
   ```

   Replace port and baud by actual board; UART ROMCODE uses 8N1, no flow control. No need to add
   port/baud to configure.
4. When the tool displays `[WAIT] UART is ready`, press RESET on GT32U2086 board.
5. ROMCODE requires each image offset, receive data, prepare Flash, burn payload, test image and then
   write the last header. Keep connection and stable power during flash.
6. Wait for `[PASS] Image transfer completed`. The tool indicates this result after receiving
   `0xFFFFFFFF` from ROMCODE and has transmitted enough image. ROMCODE continues to switch to the
   application right in this session.
7. Switch to `000` mode before the next Reset/power up to run the installed image, avoid returning to
   update pending.

The tool displays the required boot mode; it does not read or directly confirm the boot pin value on
the board. Parameter details and error handling are in
[flash firmware GT32U2086 via UART](GT32U2086Flashing.md).

sections.heading: Mode 101 — Copy from QSPI to Internal Flash
sections.text:
1. Build image profile **`normal`**, as the final application will run in
   Internal Flash.
2. Prepare image at external QSPI source. With Flash NOR which ROMCODE reads from the beginning of
   device, set all `<app>_image.bin` at `0` offset. Use programmer or loader in accordance with
   board design and re-read to confirm data.
3. Connect the QSPI power to controller/CS by board, select boot mode `101`, and then press Reset.
4. ROMCODE reads the header from QSPI source, checks the `0x00020000` image address, clears the
   necessary Internal Flash area and copies the payload to it.
5. ROMCODE checks the CRC, asks for authentication and vector, writes the final header and then
   switches to running the application in Internal Flash.
6. Check the application operation. Select mode `000` for subsequent startups if you do not want to
   repeat the update step from QSPI.

The `101` mode is not a QSPI Flash write service and does not require an XIP image. The UART 1.0
tool does not yet have a backend for preparing this QSPI source. ROMCODE does not broadcast the
`0xFFFFFFFF` UART completion message to the copy QSPI path.

sections.heading: Mode 111 — Running directly from QSPI Flash
sections.text:
1. Build image profile `xip`, use file `<app>_image_xip.bin` and check header base `0x30000000`. File
   `<app>_xip.bin` only contains payload raw.
2. Use programmer or firmware loader UART–QSPI to flash the entire image into external Flash, at `0`
   offset with image layout at the top of device. Read again to confirm contents. `0x30000000` is
   the CPU address mapped to external Flash, not the offset that must be passed to the programmer of
   the Flash chip.
3. Connect external Flash according to the board, select boot mode `111`, and then press Reset.
4. ROMCODE initializes QSPI, enables memory-mapped window and checks header, CRC configuration image,
   and application vector in XIP area.
5. If valid, ROMCODE switches to the application at QSPI Flash and keeps the XIP configuration active.
   Check LED/UART or the functionality of the application.
6. Keep `111` mode for next Reset/power-up attempts if XIP continues to run.

In the current ROMCODE, XIP lines do not perform NVR policy and signature checks like Internal lines
Flash/update. It is not inferred that the image has been authenticated with a signature only because
the XIP boot was successful.

The UART 1.0 tool does not yet provide a loader firmware for writing QSPI Flash. ROMCODE's USART
update service always writes Internal Flash and rejects XIP images. External Flash flash via UART
requires both the GT32U2086 side loader and the PC interface; adding the `--boot-mode 111` option does not
create this capability on its own.

sections.heading: Check the running firmware
sections.text:
For applications with UART logs, open the baud-based monitor that configures the application:

```sh
cmake -E env \
  NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 \
  NEON_MDF_MONITOR_BAUD=19200 \
  cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target serial_monitor
```

Application baud may differ from baud flash. The first log may appear before the monitor opens; with
normal boot mode, the monitor can be opened first and then Reset for re-observation. Do not open the
monitor simultaneously with the flashing tool on the same port.

| Phenomenon | Inspection Direction |
|---|---|
| Mode `100` without UART requirement | Boot code, Reset operation, UART flash, baud, wire TX/RX/GND |
| Mode `000` not running | Image already in Internal Flash; header, CRC, vector, NVR policy |
| Mode `101` not running | QSPI source has `normal` image at right offset; connect, image format and NVR policy |
| Mode `111` not running | Image `xip`, offset External Flash, Flash type, configuration QSPI reader and vector |
| Invalid code selected | Select one of `000`, `100`, `101`, `111` and Reset |

ROMCODE does not automatically switch to another boot source when the selected image is invalid and
does not send error code/NACK only. When a boot error occurs, check that the selected boot path is
correct because it waits for an automatic fallback mechanism.

sections.heading: Flashing GT32U2086 firmware through UART
sections.text:
GT32U2086 Flash Tool **1.0** uses ROMCODE's USART update service to burn images to Internal Flash. The
tool runs on a computer; OpenOCD is not required for this flash path.

Process for full boot lines located in
[GT32U2086 boot modes and firmware workflow](GT32U2086BootModes.md).

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.text:
**Linux/macOS:** UART flash and GT32U2086 monitor use `termios`, `select` and `os` in Python standard
library, similar to the original `uart_boot_loader.py` tool. No need to install `pyserial` or
`python3-serial` to run GT32U2086 tool when port is specified. You can go straight to connecting boards
and running flash commands.

**Windows:** tool uses `pyserial` to access COM ports. Install dependencies from the repository root
directory:

```sh
python3 -m pip install -r neon-mdf/tools/requirements.txt
```

Install in the exact Python that CMake uses to run the tool; test it on Windows with the
corresponding interpreter, for example:

```sh
python3 -c "import serial; print(serial.__version__)"
```

`pyserial` is used for the CLI SDK's automatic port detection. When
using GT32U2086 on Linux/macOS, pass the port with `--port`, `-p` or `NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT` as the
examples below so that this library is not needed.

Connect the UART flash of the board: TX of the adapter connects the RX of the board, RX connects the
TX and connects the GND together. Use the voltage level suitable for the board. Select boot mode 100
— USART update according to the foot/jumper diagram of the board. Close the other Serial Monitor
program that is holding the port before flashing.

Board needs valid NVR policy, compatible with image Secure/Non-secure. This tool does not perform
provisioning NVR. Signatures and security policies are checked by ROMCODE on the device; CRC
checking on PC does not replace that step.

sections.heading: Flash through CMake
sections.text:
Run in the application folder, for example `examples/Printf_Log/`:

```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086
```

Transfer port and baud at target flash run:

```sh
cmake -E env \
  NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 \
  NEON_MDF_SERIAL_BAUD=19200 \
  NEON_MDF_UART_BYTE_GAP_MS=2 \
  NEON_MDF_UART_LOG=full \
  cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target flash_uart_gt32u2086
```

With PowerShell or CMD, write the same command on one line and replace the port with `COM3`, for
example. `cmake -E env` passes environment variables to build and tool processes, does not store
port/baud in CMake cache. Changing these values requires no re-configuration. `cmake --build` does
not directly accept `--port`/`--baud` options.

Target builds the application itself and gets `<app>_image.bin` correctly. Do not select a `.elf` or
`.bin` file that contains only payloads. Target `flash_uart_gt32u2086` points to the first packaged
application; if the project has multiple images, select a specific `<app>_flash_uart_gt32u2086`. Projects
using `neon_mdf_add_executable()` or `neon_mdf_add_gt32u2086_image()` are registered with these targets
automatically.

The tool displays the banner including version, required boot mode, image profile, application
version, address image, port, baud and reset method. When it appears:

```text
[WAIT] Select boot mode 100 - USART update, then press RESET on the GT32U2086 board.
[WAIT] UART is ready. Press Ctrl+C to cancel.
```

Press RESET on GT32U2086 board. At this point the UART port is open and the tool is ready to reply to
ROMCODE. By default the tool waits for the first Reset until a request is received or the user
presses Ctrl+C. After transmission starts, each request has a 300 second timeout, which indicates
about how long ROMCODE pauses communication for preparing/erase Flash.

When finished:

```text
[PASS] Image transfer completed in ... seconds; total runtime ... seconds.
[INFO] ROMCODE verified and committed the image; application handoff follows.
```

The tool indicates success when ROMCODE has requested enough images and returns `0xFFFFFFFF`.
ROMCODE then switches to the application; no reset is required again to start this session.
Re-select boot mode 000 — Internal Flash before subsequent resets/powerups to run the installed
firmware.

Baud flash must match the actual ROMCODE on board. `19200` is an example; parameter indicates
PC-side UART configuration, does not change baud of ROMCODE. Transmission frame is
**8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit (8N1)**, no flow control.

sections.heading: Application monitoring
sections.text:
Baud of application independent of baud flash:

```sh
cmake -E env \
  NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 \
  NEON_MDF_MONITOR_BAUD=19200 \
  cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target serial_monitor
```

Default GT32U2086 monitor uses 19200 baud; press Ctrl+C to quit. Log `[WAIT]`, `[TX]`, `[PASS]` belong to
PC tool. The content after the application runs depends on the application itself; there is no
mandatory boot log for all firmwares. Opening the monitor after flash may miss the first log of the
application.

sections.heading: Using live tool and SDK CLI
sections.text:
From root repository:

```sh
python3 neon-mdf/tools/gt32u2086_flash.py --version
python3 neon-mdf/tools/gt32u2086_flash.py --list-boot-modes
python3 neon-mdf/tools/gt32u2086_flash.py --image /path/to/my_app_image.bin --check-only
python3 neon-mdf/tools/gt32u2086_flash.py \
  --port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baud 19200 \
  --image /path/to/my_app_image.bin \
  --monitor --monitor-baud 19200
```

The tool receives `.bin` or `.hex`/`.mem` tokens as byte/word; this is not an Intel HEX parser. Use
`--hex-format byte|word` if you need to specify the interpretation. `--byte-gap-ms` defaults to 2 ms
for reply bytes, just like the original `uart_boot_loader.py` tool. Log shows each request and
response by default:

```text
[RX #1] 00 00 00 00  request offset=0x00000000
[TX] 55 54 50 46  image[0x00000000:0x00000004]  0.0%
[RX #2] 04 00 00 00  request offset=0x00000004
[TX] ...  image[0x00000004:0x00000008]  ...%
```

The tool returns all 4 bytes in offset, write log with separate stream after response so that the
terminal display does not block the transmission loop. Do not check/cancel TX between bytes of the
same word. If ROMCODE requests to re-offset, the tool sends back the correct word. You can choose
`--log-mode progress` or `--quiet` to view only percentages; `--verbose` is equivalent to
`--log-mode full`.

`--timeout` replaces the requested timeout; `--wait-timeout` limits the first Reset timeout. By
default, when the flash is finished, exit, only open the monitor if there is `--monitor`.

sections.heading: Adjustable transmission speed
sections.text:
Parameters read at runtime, no need to configure again:

| Environment variable | Optional live tool | Default value |
|---|---|---|
| `NEON_MDF_UART_BYTE_GAP_MS` | `--byte-gap-ms` | `2` ms |
| `NEON_MDF_UART_LOG` | `--log-mode` | `full` (each RX/TX); or `progress` |

Each 4 byte word has 3 gaps. With 31.476 bytes and 2 ms gap image, the rest time on the PC combined
was about 47 seconds, not counting UART transmission, USB and Flash operation of ROMCODE. This is
also how to stretch bytes of the original tool.

To try to reduce downtime, it is possible to pass `NEON_MDF_UART_BYTE_GAP_MS=0` in CMake command, or
`--byte-gap-ms 0` when calling the tool directly. When the gap is zero, the tool sends the whole
word with one write. The appropriate value depends on FIFO/clock and the actual board; if a retry or
CRC appears that does not match, return to the 2 ms gap in use stably. Flash speed also depends on
the time of writing Flash and ROMCODE requires each word, so it is necessary to measure the
completion time on the board.

From the application directory, after having set `NEON_MDF_PATH`:

```sh
python3 "$NEON_MDF_PATH/tools/neon_mdf.py" \
  -t GT32U2086 -p /dev/ttyUSB0 -b 19200 flash-uart-gt32u2086
```

CLI calls the same CMake target; can append `monitor` and `--monitor-baud 19200` actions before the
action list.

sections.heading: Boot modes and XIP images
sections.text:
| Boot mode | ROMCODE Activity | The role of the UART 1.0 tool |
|---|---|---|
| `000` | Check and run image already in Internal Flash | No UART image receiving service |
| `100` | Get image via UART and record Internal Flash | flash image profile `normal` |
| `101` | Read image from external QSPI source and update Internal Flash | Need to prepare QSPI source by corresponding tool |
| `111` | Check and run image in QSPI XIP area | Need flash External Flash by programmer or loader UART–QSPI |

The XIP image has a base `0x30000000`, while the Internal Flash image has a base `0x00020000`. The
tool can check both profiles with `--check-only`, but will refuse to transmit the XIP image using
USART update service before opening UART port. Replacing `--boot-mode` only describes the required
mode, does not control the boot pin and does not add QSPI recording service to ROMCODE.

sections.heading: Using the VS Code extension
sections.text:
1. Use **Select Port** to choose the board's UART port.
2. Set `neonMdf.gt32u2086FlashBaudRate` to match ROMCODE and `neonMdf.baudRate`
   to match the application. Both default to 19200.
3. Use **Flash**. The extension releases any open monitor session before running
   the SDK upload task.
4. Select boot mode 100, wait until the tool reports that UART is ready, then press RESET.
5. An open monitor session is restored after a successful upload. Use **Monitor**
   to open one manually, or **Build + Flash + Log** to open it automatically
   after programming.

See the [VS Code guide](VSCode.md) for installation and the remaining commands.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
| Phenomenon | Inspection |
|---|---|
| Missing port/baud | Transmit `NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT` and `NEON_MDF_SERIAL_BAUD` in flash command |
| Cannot open port | Port Name, Access and Other Serial Monitor Programs |
| Waiting for Reset but no data | Boot mode 100, connect TX/RX/GND, baud and Reset operation |
| `[RETRY]` | ROMCODE asks for resubmission; if prolonged, check connection, baud and byte spacing |
| Timeout after header | ROMCODE may be preparing Flash or has rejected image; check Flash timeout and configuration |
| Full byte transmission but no `[PASS]` | ROMCODE not confirmed complete; check CRC, signature, NVR policy and connection |
| Image XIP rejected | Use external QSPI Flash path; USART update only write Internal Flash |

ROMCODE does not send NACK/error codes only. Tool will report timeout, not deduce specific security
reasons or report success based on transmission percentage only.

sections.heading: GT32U2086 support and hardware acceptance
sections.text:
The SDK contains implemented examples and automated host build checks.
Hardware acceptance requires measurements on the specific board and bitstream.
Retain these with the firmware revision; a build, local image check or timeout
path alone does not establish peripheral hardware validation.

| Module | Example or API | Acceptance evidence and limits |
|---|---|---|
| GPIO | Input/output and IRQ | PB5/PB7 routing, pull-up, edge count and debounce |
| UART/console | Polling, IRQ, printf | Baud/frame timing, RX/TX data, errors and idle |
| UART DMA | TX/RX menu | Word-per-character peripheral profile and timeout recovery remain incomplete; compare against the hardware USART DMA contract |
| I2C | EEPROM, DMA and slave APIs | Unshifted addresses, repeated START, NACK, pull-ups and DMA requests; no standalone slave example |
| SPI | W5500 polling and DMA | VERSIONR, restored register patterns, 32-byte SRAM comparison, CS hold and request routing |
| TIM/PWM | Periodic IRQ and PWM | Output period and live STT duration; software flag clear unsupported on the current FPGA backend |
| ADC | 1/4/16-sample batches | Input range, channel route, sample count and saturation; CPU processing uses whole words |
| RTC | Calendar menu | Readback, five second increments, minute/leap-day/year rollover, invalid inputs and RTC source/prescaler |
| CRC | Six vector/boundary tests | CRC-8 polynomial `0x07`, all 32 bits per input word MSB first; length counts words |
| AES | ECB encrypt/decrypt | FIPS-197 vector and native word order; CBC/CTR need protocol-specific vectors |
| TRNG | Polling and digital BIST | FPGA timeouts and LFSR BIST do not validate silicon entropy quality |
| Internal Flash | Reserved-sector read/write | Erase/program/readback and overlap protection; NVR provisioning is separate |
| QSPI | Indirect NOR and mapped reads | JEDEC ID, QE/status, scratch region and original-pattern comparison; DDR/DMA/automatic status polling unsupported |
| WDT | Public driver APIs | Refresh and deliberate expiry/reset; no dedicated standalone example |
| FreeRTOS | Blinky and peripheral queue | Tick, preemption, IRQ forwarding, stack/heap margins and ownership |
| JTAG | Attach integration point | OpenOCD is a placeholder; use a verified board/probe configuration |

There is no `FPGA_Terminal`, `DMA_Memory_Copy`, `I2C_Register_Read_Write`,
`I2C_Slave` or `QSPI_Flash_Indirect` project. The [example index](../examples/README.md)
lists actual project and firmware names.

sections.heading: Record a board result
sections.text:
Retain the SDK revision, board/bitstream, toolchain, profile, clock source,
`sdkconfig`, image version/hash, boot mode, wiring, UART log and scope/logic
captures. Record expected/observed values, recovery and final pass/fail.
For DMA, verify completion and bus retirement before reusing buffers. SPI DMA
parks incomplete commands and requires reset before another run; parking and
timeout are not acknowledged aborts.

sections.heading: Automated checks
sections.text:
Install normal Python requirements plus `cryptography`, then run:

```sh
python .github/scripts/validate_sdk.py
```

The CI runner copies applications to a temporary directory and checks all
examples, both templates, image header/size/CRC/vectors, selected Release builds,
CLI/CMake configuration refresh, concurrent normal/XIP directories and signing.
It never opens UART or provisions NVR. Build logs remain in the printed location;
`--work-dir build/validation` selects an empty destination.

Its conservative instruction audit rejects byte/halfword load/store candidates
