in CMake firmware objects, including the vendored kernel. Legitimate Flash/MMIO
accesses require explicit review. It does not prove address ranges or inspect
prebuilt toolchain libraries. `.github/workflows/sdk.yml` runs these checks and
the VS Code TypeScript build; validation scripts are kept outside SDK tools.

sections.heading: Optional declaration `menuconfig`/`sdkconfig`
sections.text:
Instructions for adding 1 toggle options via `menuconfig` — are the same as ESP-IDF's
`Kconfig`/`sdkconfig` system (reused with `kconfiglib`, no parser). See [Architecture](Architecture.md) for a design overview; this file goes into the option declaration syntax + usage.

sections.heading: General Models
sections.text:
```
neon-mdf/Kconfig                      # mainmenu SDK - rsource each component
  └─ components/driver/Kconfig         # option OF SDK
  └─ osource "$(NEON_MDF_APP_KCONFIG)" # option OF APP (if app has its own Kconfig)

<app>/Kconfig     # OPTIONS - separate app options, automatically merged into THE SAME menu
<app>/sdkconfig   # Selected configuration (text file, versioned with the application)
        │ (cmake/kconfig.cmake -> tools/kconfig/gen_config_header.py, run at configure)
        ▼
build/<TARGET>/config/sdkconfig.h      # #define CONFIG_X ... - used in C code
build/<TARGET>/config/sdkconfig.cmake  # set(CONFIG_X ...) - used in CMakeLists.txt
```

Option SDK (`components/driver/Kconfig`) and option app (`<app>/Kconfig`, if available) ** combine 1
menu, 1 `sdkconfig` file** — app does not need to know anything about the merge mechanism, just
create a `Kconfig` file next to your `CMakeLists.txt` (see section 3).

sections.heading: 1. 1 option declaration syntax
sections.text:
Standard Kconfig syntax (identical to Linux kernel/ESP-IDF/Zephyr — `kconfiglib` read directly, no
separate syntax of this SDK):

```kconfig
menu "current menu name"

config TEN_OPTION
    bool "open ta shortcut shown in menuconfig"
    default y
    help
        open us long, this option stage is nothing, the image direction so.

config TEN_OPTION_SO
    int "Number of loop iterations ..."
    default 500000
    help
        ...

endmenu
```

| Type | Syntax `default` | generated in `sdkconfig.h` | generated in `sdkconfig.cmake` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bool` | `default y` \| `default n` | `#define CONFIG_TEN_OPTION 1` (only if `y`, NO `#define` if `n` — use `#ifdef`, not `#if`) | `set(CONFIG_TEN_OPTION ON)` \| `OFF` |
| `int` | `default 500000` | `#define CONFIG_TEN_OPTION 500000` | `set(CONFIG_TEN_OPTION 500000)` |
| `hex` | `default 0x1000` | `#define CONFIG_TEN_OPTION 0x1000` | `set(CONFIG_TEN_OPTION 0x1000)` |
| `string` | `default "abc"` | `#define CONFIG_TEN_OPTION "abc"` | `set(CONFIG_TEN_OPTION "abc")` |

The option name in Kconfig (`TEN_OPTION`) **no prefix** — macro/variable generated automatically
adds `CONFIG_` (identical to ESP-IDF convention). Name the SDK option with a prefix `NEON_MDF_`
(e.g. `NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART`) so that it does not match the app's option; app options do not need
this prefix (e.g. `BLINKY_DELAY_LOOPS`).

Real example (`components/driver/Kconfig`):

```kconfig
menu "components/driver"

config NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART
    bool "Compile the UART driver (uart/neon_uart.c)"
    default y
    help
        warn UART driver gathering in build. disable to reduce Flash usage if app does not use UART - in
        that case uart/neon_uart.c is not compile.

endmenu
```

sections.heading: 2. Used in C code
sections.text:
```c
#include "sdkconfig.h"

#if defined(CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART)
  /* only translate variables when option BOOL is enabled */
#endif

#define DELAY_LOOPS CONFIG_BLINKY_DELAY_LOOPS /* option INT use directly as the number */
```

`sdkconfig.h` is included in include path (target `neon_mdf_kconfig`, already linked to
`neon_mdf_driver` PUBLIC — all `neon_mdf_driver` app links are `#include "sdkconfig.h"` right away,
no need to add anything in the `CMakeLists.txt` of the app).

sections.heading: 3. Used in `CMakeLists.txt` (power file on/off)
sections.text:
```cmake
if(CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART)
  list(APPEND _neon_mdf_driver_sources uart/neon_uart.c)
endif()
```

The `CONFIG_*` variable is valid only AFTER `neon_mdf_process_kconfig()` (`cmake/kconfig.cmake`) has
run — in `components/driver/CMakeLists.txt`. This is always possible because
`neon-mdf/CMakeLists.txt` calls this function BEFORE `add_subdirectory(components/driver)` (see
`guide/ArchitectDetail.md` section 4 for full order). This is the mechanism `components/driver` uses
to NOT compile a file `.c` when the option is disabled (see `guide/DriverImplement.md` section 3,
dispatch type (c)) — does not "hide feature at runtime", the app that calls the disabled function
will have a clear link error (`undefined reference`), not a hidden error.

sections.heading: 4. Add new option for SDK (component available)
sections.text:
Straighten `components/driver/Kconfig` (add 1 new block `config ...` in the existing `menu`). No
need to edit `neon-mdf/Kconfig` (this file is already `rsource`).

sections.heading: 5. Add Kconfig to app (option of 1 example)
sections.text:
Create `<app>/Kconfig` next to `<app>/CMakeLists.txt` — **don't need to edit the app's
`CMakeLists.txt`** to "enable" this feature (same as `osource` = Make's `-include` style, auto merge
if file exists, silent ignore otherwise — old behavior of app without this file stays 100%):

```kconfig
menu "App name (this app)"

config MY_APP_SOME_OPTION
    int "Option description"
    default 1000
    help
        ...

endmenu
```

read in `Src/main.c` via `#include "sdkconfig.h"` + `CONFIG_MY_APP_SOME_OPTION` identical to SDK
option — can not distinguish (and does not need to distinguish) which option comes from the SDK or
app in code using it.

sections.heading: 6. Open menuconfig — edit value
sections.text:
```sh
cd examples/Blinky
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target menuconfig   # open UI select (same as idf.py menuconfig)
cmake --preset GT32U2086                                 # mandatory re-configure after saving to apply
```

Or via VS Code: command **NEON-MDF: menuconfig**. Or CLI: `neon_mdf.py menuconfig`. All 3 paths call
the same target CMake `menuconfig` (`cmake/kconfig.cmake`) — without any other logic in UI layer.

It is also possible to edit manually `<app>/sdkconfig` (text file, like ESP-IDF) and then `cmake
--preset <TARGET>` again — for example disable UART:

```
# CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART is not set
```

`sdkconfig` records itself every time it configures (resembles ESP-IDF): new options added to
Kconfig autofill `default` into the file, options that no longer exist in Kconfig (deleted from
`.Kconfig` file) are automatically removed from `sdkconfig` — no manual removal of this file is
required when changing the option structure.

sections.heading: Checklist added a new option
sections.text:
1. Determine if it belongs to the SDK (fixing `components/driver/Kconfig`, or a new `Kconfig` file for
   another component + adding `rsource` in `neon-mdf/Kconfig`) or if it belongs to an app alone
   (`<app>/Kconfig`, automatically merged, no further fixes).
2. Choosing the right `type` (`bool`/`int`/`hex`/`string`) — decides usage in C (`#ifdef` for `bool`,
   direct value for `int`/`hex`/`string`).
3. Set rational `default` — app build for the first time (without `sdkconfig`) use YES this value, not
   empty/0.
4. If used to enable/disable compile 1 file `.c` — add `if(CONFIG_...)` in the right place in the
   relevant `CMakeLists.txt` (see section 3).
5. `cmake --preset <TARGET>` back (configure) so that `sdkconfig.h`/`.cmake` generated Kconfig matches
   new — old build (`build/`) does not update itself.

sections.heading: Automatic build refresh
sections.text:
CMake tracks `sdkconfig`, sourced Kconfig files and the configuration generator.
The next CLI or direct CMake build applies saved settings automatically.
The explicit configure steps above remain valid and are useful when inspecting
configuration output. Changing a compiler, interpreter or build profile still
requires an explicit configure; use separate build directories for profiles.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text:
This document defines source organization, naming, header/source layout, Doxygen, API design and review rules for NEON Extension. It defines the conventions used by the GT32U2086 SDK.

Key NEON decisions:

- HAL public functions: `neon_<module>_<action>()`.
- Public types: `neon_<module>_<name>_t`; cross-module types: `neon_<name>_t`.
- Header guards: `__NEON_<MODULE>_H__` (project-specific exception; identifiers beginning `__` are reserved by ISO C/C++).
- File names, variables, and HAL public functions: lowercase `snake_case`.
- Opening braces on the same line; four-space indentation.

sections.heading: 2. Source Folder And File Convention
sections.text:
| Item | Format | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Common entry header | `neon.h` | `neon.h` |
| Common types | `neon_types.h` | `neon_types.h` |
| Configuration | `neon_config.h` | `neon_config.h` |
| HAL module | `neon_<module>.c/.h` | `neon_uart.c`, `neon_uart.h` |
| Internal header | `neon_<module>_internal.h` | `neon_uart_internal.h` |
| SoC register header | `neon_<module>_regs.h` | `neon_uart_regs.h` |
| Shared core helper | `neon_<module>_core.c/.h` | `neon_qspi_core.c` |
| Utility | `neon_utils_<name>.c/.h` | `neon_utils_crc.c` |
| Test | `test_neon_<module>.c` | `test_neon_uart.c` |

One driver module normally has one public header and matching implementation. Hardware variants belong in platform-specific directories unless their public functionality actually differs. Do not edit third-party code merely to satisfy naming rules; isolate it behind NEON wrappers.

sections.heading: 3. Naming Convention
sections.text:
| Item | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| HAL public function | `neon_<module>_<action>()` | `neon_uart_transmit()` |
| Private function | `<module>_<action>()` | `uart_wait_tx_ready()` |
| Handle type | `neon_<module>_handle_t` | `neon_uart_handle_t` |
| Configuration type | `neon_<module>_config_t` | `neon_uart_config_t` |
| Other struct | `neon_<module>_<name>_t` | `neon_uart_stats_t` |
| Enum type | `neon_<module>_<name>_t` | `neon_uart_state_t` |
| Enum value | `NEON_<MODULE>_<VALUE>` | `NEON_UART_STATE_BUSY` |
| Shared/common type | `neon_<name>_t` | `neon_status_t` |
| Callback typedef | `neon_<module>_<event>_callback_t` | `neon_uart_event_callback_t` |
| Public macro | `NEON_<MODULE>_<NAME>` | `NEON_UART_FIFO_SIZE` |
| Private macro | `<MODULE>_<NAME>` | `UART_TX_RETRY_LIMIT` |
| Parameter/field/local | `snake_case` | `baud_rate`, `timeout_ms` |
| Public global (avoid if possible) | `neon_<module>_<name>` | `neon_uart_default_config` |
| Header guard | `__NEON_<MODULE>_H__` | `__NEON_UART_H__` |

sections.heading: 3.1 Types And Structs
3.2 Enums And Bitmasks
3.3 Common Status
3.4 Function Verbs And Modes
sections.text:
| Verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `init` / `deinit` | Create/reset driver runtime context | `neon_uart_init()` |
| `set_config` / `get_config` | Apply/read peripheral configuration | `neon_uart_set_config()` |
| `enable` / `disable` | Toggle feature | `neon_uart_enable()` |
| `start` / `stop` | Start/stop processing | `neon_timer_start()` |
| `read` / `write` | Memory/register/device operations | `neon_flash_read()` |
| `transmit` / `receive` | Streaming data operation | `neon_uart_transmit()` |
| `get_state` / `get_error` | Read runtime diagnostics | `neon_uart_get_state()` |
| `register_callback` | Register a callback | `neon_uart_register_callback()` |

Use `_IT` and `_DMA` suffixes only for genuine interrupt/DMA processing variants. Avoid synonyms such as `Send` and `Transmit` for the same operation in one module. Private helpers are `static`, use `snake_case`, and do not use `static_` in their names.

sections.heading: 3.5 Parameters, Macros And Constants
sections.text:
- Name quantities with units where ambiguity is possible: `timeout_ms`, `frequency_hz`, `size_bytes`.
- Input pointers not modified by the callee must point to `const` data.
- Use `U`, `UL` or `ULL` integer suffixes appropriate to the type.
- Prefer `static inline` over side-effecting or multi-line function-like macros.
- Avoid public mutable globals and magic numbers.
- Never prefix new C identifiers with an underscore except for the explicitly chosen legacy-style header guards.

sections.heading: 4. Header File Format
5. Source File Format
6. Comment And Doxygen Convention
sections.text:
Document every public API with `@brief`, `@param[in]` / `[out]` / `[in,out]` and `@return` (when non-void). Use `@details`, `@note`, and `@warning` as appropriate. Document units, valid ranges, blocking behavior, ISR eligibility, thread safety and ownership when relevant.

```c
/**
 * @brief      Transmit data using UART polling mode.
 * @param[in]  huart       Initialized UART handle.
 * @param[in]  data        Data buffer to transmit.
 * @param[in]  size_bytes  Number of bytes to transmit.
 * @param[in]  timeout_ms  Maximum wait time in milliseconds.
 * @return     NEON_OK on success, otherwise the error status.
 * @note       This function blocks until completion, timeout or error.
 */
neon_status_t neon_uart_transmit(neon_uart_handle_t *huart, const uint8_t *data,
                                 uint32_t size_bytes, uint32_t timeout_ms);
```

Do not add `@param None` for functions without parameters. Private helpers need comments when the intent or register side effects are not obvious.

sections.heading: 7. Include And Configuration Convention
sections.text:
Use `neon_config.h` for compile-time features; name switches `NEON_<MODULE>_MODULE_ENABLED` and use consistent 0/1 values:

```c
#define NEON_UART_MODULE_ENABLED  1
#define NEON_SPI_MODULE_ENABLED   1
#define NEON_USE_ASSERT           1

#if defined(NEON_UART_MODULE_ENABLED) && (NEON_UART_MODULE_ENABLED == 1)
/* UART build-dependent declarations/implementation. */
#endif
```

Keep peripheral clock, pinmux and board frequencies in SoC/board configuration files. Public headers should not require unrelated application configuration to parse. `neon.h` may aggregate enabled public module headers, but individual headers remain independently includable.

sections.heading: 8. Platform And Build Organization
sections.text:
- Keep device registers, startup, linker scripts and interrupt-vector integration in SoC/platform directories.
- Place generated artifacts under the firmware project's build/release folders, not within driver source directories.
- Use warning flags, static analysis and target-specific builds to check portability.
- Test a module under every supported SoC/compiler combination it claims to support.
- A HAL handle shall have a documented single owner. When ISR, tasks or both cores access the same instance, define synchronization and memory-order guarantees explicitly.
- Polling APIs shall use bounded timeouts where appropriate; no blocking waits inside ISR. ROM-only LL code can use deterministic bounded loops when no time base exists.

sections.heading: 9. New Module Checklist
sections.text:
| Step | Check |
|---:|---|
| 1 | Choose HAL, LL, utility, or SoC layer with allowed dependencies |
| 2 | Name files `neon_<module>` |
| 3 | Add `__NEON_<MODULE>_H__` header guard |
| 4 | Use `neon_<module>_` for HAL functions; `NEON_<MODULE>_` for enum values and macros |
| 5 | Use `neon_<module>_<name>_t` for exported types |
| 6 | Add file header, section banners and Doxygen public APIs |
| 7 | Keep private functions `static` and `snake_case` |
| 8 | Check struct ownership, configuration/state separation |
| 9 | Check pointer `const`, units, bounds and error handling |
| 10 | Check ISR behavior, timeout, concurrent access and register side effects |
| 11 | Add feature flag only when build-time optionality is needed |
| 12 | Build, test and verify header self-containment |

sections.heading: 10. Module Templates And API Lifecycle

documents.title: Neon MDF — Source Format & Convention V1.3

sections.heading: Neon MDF — Source Format & Convention V1.3
1. Purpose and scope
sections.text:
Neon MDF applies the [NEON Coding Convention V1.3](NEON_Coding_Convention_V1.3.md) to handwritten
C/header in SDK, templates and examples. This file describes how conventions are applied to existing
Neon MDF structure, build and hardware.

Main convention: public HAL API `neon_module_action()`, private helper `module_action()`, type `_t`,
field `snake_case`, indent 4 spaces and open brackets same line. The private helper keeps the
keyword `static`.

Device register type, name register, startup/linker symbol, `main`, ISR, `SystemInit`,
`SystemCoreClock`, syscall/runtime and FreeRTOS hook keep the platform contract.
GT32U2086 uses CMSIS directly. Vendor source and generated output are not reformatted only for style.

sections.heading: 2. Repository structure
sections.text:
```text
<repository>/
├── .clang-format
├── .clang-format-ignore
├── neon-mdf/
│   ├── components/
│   │   ├── driver/                 # HAL and peripheral backend
│   │   └── console/                # printf/console GT32U2086
│   ├── arch/                       # CPU, device, IRQ, runtime
│   ├── mcu-description/            # YAML, schema, generator
│   ├── cmake/                      # Toolchain and build integration
│   ├── tools/                      # CLI, templates, audit and test
│   └── rtos/FreeRTOS-Kernel/        # Upstream and patch platforms
├── examples/<App>/                 # Independent CMake Project
└── guide/
```

SDK/app structure and dimensional dependency are further described in
[Architecture](Architecture.md).

sections.heading: 3. Architecture and dependencies
sections.text:
App calls component/HAL; backends API mapping to register, clock, reset and pinmux of family. Driver
does not include `main.h` or source app dependencies. Header uses `mcu_device.h` or header
`neon_<module>_device.h` respectively to get type/instance of selected device.

CMake selects backend according to `NEON_MDF_TARGET_<TARGET>_FAMILY`. Cortex-M enables/disables IRQ
and sets priority via CMSIS `NVIC_*`; critical sections save/restore PRIMASK.
The required Flash/reset operation on GT32U2086 runs from SRAM.

sections.heading: 4. Directory and file source conventions
sections.text:
| Ingredients | Current path/template |
|---|---|
| Entry header optional | `components/driver/neon.h` |
| Common Type | `components/driver/neon_types.h` |
| Module switches | `components/driver/neon_config.h` |
| Header HAL | `components/driver/<module>/neon_<module>.h` |
| Header instance | `<module>/neon_<module>_device.h`, when API needs alias instance |
| Backend | `<module>/platform/<family>/neon_<module>.c` |
| Internal header by platform | `syscsr/platform/gt32u2086/neon_syscsr_internal.h` |
| GT32U2086 internal memory utility | `components/driver/neon_utils_memory.h` |
| Source/header app | `examples/<App>/Src/`, `Inc/`; standalone FPGA examples follow `Printf_Log` |
| Standalone FPGA peripheral example | `examples/<Example>/` |

For example:

```text
components/driver/uart/
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── neon_uart.h
├── neon_uart_device.h
└── platform/
    └── gt32u2086/neon_uart.c
```

The file name uses lowercase letters and underscores. Existing example directory names such
as `UART_RX_Interrupt` and `CRC_Known_Vector` are retained. Each GT32U2086 example has its own `Src/main.c`
and executable. Add implementation files to CMake sources; do not include a `.c` file directly.

sections.heading: 5. Naming convention
sections.text:
| Ingredients | Format/example |
|---|---|
| Public HAL function | `neon_uart_transmit()`, `neon_flash_erase_sector()` |
| Private function | `static ... uart_wait_tx_ready(...)` |
| Handle | `neon_uart_handle_t` |
| Configuration | `neon_uart_config_t` |
| Struct/enum Other | `neon_uart_state_t`, `neon_spi_fifo_config_t` |
| Common Type | `neon_status_t`, `neon_field8_t`, `neon_field16_t` |
| Named struct tag | `neon_uart_handle_s` if need to put tag |
| Enum value/public macro | `NEON_UART_STATE_READY`, `NEON_GPIO_PIN_7` |
| Private macro | `UART_CONTEXT_PIN_AUTO`, `FLASH_RAMFUNC` |
| Field/parameter/local | `baud_rate`, `clock_frequency_hz`, `timeout_polls` |
| Header guard | `__NEON_UART_H__` by choice of V1.3 |

Private helper does not add `static_` to the name. HAL's type uses `_t`; type register like
`UART_TypeDef` remains device generator of the same level. Internal interface by platform can
network namespace family, for example `gt32u2086_syscsr_*`; application does not use internal headers.

Public enum with explicit value, preserving existing encoding. Use unsigned macro for combining
bitmasks. Keep literal `U`, `UL`, `ULL` by width. Input pointer is not modified using `const`.
Failable operations usually return `neon_status_t`; keep meaning of existing statuses, including
`NEON_NOT_SUPPORTED`, `NEON_LOCKED`, `NEON_NOT_MAPPED`.

sections.heading: 6. Format header
sections.text:
Order: Doxygen file → include guard → include necessary → type/macro → public prototype → close C++
guard and include guard. Use banner section as current files; only create section with content.

The header itself provides dependencies for its declaration and can be used independently of the
family that the module supports. Wrap external declarations with conditional `extern "C"`. Private
variables/helpers are in `.c`; internal write header `@internal`.

```c
#ifndef __NEON_EXAMPLE_H__
#define __NEON_EXAMPLE_H__

#include "neon_types.h"

#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif

/**
 * @brief Initialize the example module.
 * @return NEON_OK on success, otherwise a module error status.
 */
neon_status_t neon_example_init(void);

#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif

#endif /* __NEON_EXAMPLE_H__ */
```

sections.heading: 7. Format source
sections.text:
Source includes the corresponding public header first; followed by dependency private/platform and
standard library. The file was moved to `platform/` include header using a module path like
`"uart/neon_uart.h"`.

Section order:

1. `INCLUDE FILES`
2. `DEFINES AND MACROS` when available
3. `STRUCTURES AND OTHER TYPEDEFS` when available
4. `LOCAL VARIABLES` when available
5. `PRIVATE FUNCTION PROTOTYPES` when available
6. `GLOBAL FUNCTIONS`
7. `PRIVATE FUNCTIONS` when available

Use 4 spaces, open brackets on the same line, with brackets for all `if/else/for/while`. Do not
merge functions, loops or conditional branches into a single line. Declare helper before caller.
File `.c` compiled in C does not need `extern "C"` blocks.

`.clang-format` at root encodes the presentation rules, including `InsertBraces` and recommendation
column 120. `.clang-format-ignore` removes build, upstream and output hardware generator from batch
format operations.

sections.heading: 8. Comment and Doxygen
sections.text:
The file has `@file`, `@brief`, `@details`. The public API is described at the header with `@brief`,
`@param[in/out/in,out]`, `@return` when non-void. Use `@details`, `@note` when interpreting
blocking, ISR, thread safety, ownership and side effect of registers. Implementation uses `@copydoc`
to reuse contracts.

Do not add `@param None`. Comment focuses on reasons and hardware contracts, specifically timeout,
read-to-clear/W1C, buffer, pinmux and reset order.

sections.heading: 9. configuration and include
sections.text:
`neon_config.h` offers the `NEON_<MODULE>_MODULE_ENABLED` switch as **0/1**. The default switches
reflect the family and `sdkconfig` of the build; it is possible to override the switch before
including the header. `neon.h` is an optional entry header for including on modules. Each module's
include header remains independent.

```c
#include "neon_config.h"

#if NEON_UART_MODULE_ENABLED == 1
#include "uart/neon_uart.h"
#endif
```

Kconfig/menuconfig is still the source of SDK build selection. CMake reads
`CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_<MODULE>` to add a source; `neon_config.h` passes that selection onto the C
switch 0/1. Override switch in source does not automatically add disabled drivers to the library:
when changing features, update the corresponding Kconfig/build. HAL headers do not require the app's
own configuration just to parse declarations.

Details: [MenuConfig.md](MenuConfig.md).

sections.heading: 10. Handle, configuration and platform
11. Checklist and Inspection
sections.text:
- Select correct component/module and backend family.
- Use the name file/API/type/field and guard according to V1.3.
- Test independent headers, C++ guard and Doxygen of API.
- Update all calls, CMake, templates and tests when changing interface/path.
- Check owner, input `const`, unit, bounds, timeout, ISR and side effect.
- Handwritten format source; retains register/runtime/upstream contract.
- Build related targets, run meaningful regression for changes.
- With GT32U2086 test word-access, SRAM placement and emulation; emulation does not validate FPGA timing or
  actual hardware.

```sh
. neon-mdf/export.sh
cd examples/SPI_W5500
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

How to add driver: [DriverImplement.md](DriverImplement.md).

documents.title: Export log using printf on GT32U2086

sections.heading: Export log using printf on GT32U2086
sections.text:
GT32U2086 has a compact `printf` set, outputting via the `_write` syscall hook, without newlib's heap or
stdio. The formatter uses 32-bit word access to match GT32U2086 SRAM. For GT32U2086, only the
`CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART` flag enables both the UART driver and `printf/_write`.
There is no separate printf flag.

sections.heading: Use in app
sections.text:
Build using the SDK's project helpers. The `<stdio.h>` header provides standard declarations; the
SDK provides implementations of `printf`, `vprintf`, `puts` and `putchar`. Enable UART in sdkconfig:

```text
CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART=y
```

No need to manually write `_write()` or enable a different printf flag. When UART is turned off,
drivers and consoles are not compiled; the app that calls printf will report link errors. App only
needs to include `<stdio.h>` and then call `printf`. First output manually initialize UART0 at 19200
baud, 8N1, using the startup setup `SystemCoreClock`.

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    if (printf("[INFO] counter=%u status=0x%08lX\n", 1U, 0x1234UL) < 0) {
        /* Log failure; can be checked by debugger. */
    }
    for (;;) { }
}
```

The startup clock must match the board. For example, `Printf_Log` uses a 10 MHz fixed FPGA clock.
The console manually turns on/reset UART0 and configuration baud at the first write; it does not
automatically change the system-wide clock policy.

If another UART/baud is needed, it can be include `console/neon_console.h`, initialize a `static`
handle according to the application configuration and invoke `neon_console_attach_uart()` before
printing. This API is optional; only accepts READY handles, 8-bit word lengths, and non-zero
timeouts. The handle must exist for the duration of the attach. Invoke `neon_console_detach_uart()`
before deinit that handle; next print returns to default UART0. Other UART0 transactions must
coordinate with the console; the first printf can reset UART0 if the application handle has not been
attached yet.

sections.heading: Mechanism of operation
sections.text:
1. when the family is GT32U2086 and `CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_UART=y`, CMake puts
   `components/console/platform/gt32u2086/neon_console.c` and
   `components/driver/uart/platform/gt32u2086/neon_uart.c` into `neon_mdf_driver` library. There is no
   separate printf flag.
2. `<stdio.h>` declares `printf`. when the app calls a function, the linker takes the SDK
   implementation from the driver library. GT32U2086 links to `-nostdlib` and uses the SDK formatter, not
   newlib's stdio formatter.
3. `printf` collect arguments using `va_list`, call `vprintf`, then formatter analyze `%s`, `%d`, `%x`,
   width/precision… and generate each character.
4. `emit` puts the character in a 32-bit aligned word, then calls `_write(1, data, 1)`. `_write`
   initializes UART0 itself if no handle console is available, changes LF to CRLF, and calls HAL
   UART. stdout (`file=1`) and stderr (`file=2`) share the same console.
5. Driver UART polling for TX ready, write character to register THR; hardware UART outputs bits to the
   TX pin according to the configured baud. USB-UART and Serial Monitor receive byte streams and
   display them as text.

`neon_console_attach_uart` is the optional way to see the default UART, not the required step before
printf. `_write` is the console's general output layer. Functions not used by the app can be removed
from the firmware by the linker using `--gc-sections`; with UART enabled, the printf API is
available without additional flags.

sections.heading: Syscall hook on bare-metal
sections.text:
With newlib, the output stream is usually `printf → stdio → _write → UART`. `_write` is a C function
whose firmware is the same level as the C library; on bare-metal it does not necessarily call the
kernel or issue SVC commands. It can call HAL UART or polling and write straight register TX,
depending on the backend.

GT32U2086 uses its own formatter because SRAM only supports word aligned access. Only `_write` can be
found, but not byte/halfword in newlib's formatter, buffer and backend functions. Current
implementation is
`printf → vprintf → formatter word-only → _write → HAL UART → TX`.
The app does not need to call drivers; inside the SDK, `_write` reuses HAL to manage
clock/reset/pinmux/baud and timeout, without repeating register logic.

Direct call `_write` returns the number of bytes input consumed, may partially count when UART fails
after sending data, or `-1` when no bytes have been sent. `neon_console_get_status()` explains the
error; this bare-metal backend does not set up newlib's errno. The buffer transmitted to `_write`
must own all word aligned containing it, like other GT32U2086 buffers.

sections.heading: Format and behavior
sections.text:
| Supports | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| String, Character, Mark `%` | `%s`, `%c`, `%%` |
| Integer signed/unsigned | `%d`, `%i`, `%u` |
| Hex and octal | `%x`, `%X`, `%o`, `%08lX`, `%#x` |
| pointer | `%p` — always prefixed with `0x`, including pointer null |
| Integer length | `hh`, `h`, `l`, `ll`, `z` |
| Margins, marks, padding | `-`, `+`, space, `#`, `0` |
| Width/precision | `%8.3s`, `%*.*d`; each field max 1024 |

No floats are supported (`%f/%e/%g/...`), `%n`, wide characters, positional arguments or the entire
stdio library (`fprintf`, `snprintf`, `scanf`, `fflush`, ...). No `setvbuf()` is needed instead of
`fflush()`: each character is sent immediately using UART polling. Do not add newlib stdio to extend
these functions on GT32U2086, because those lines do not guarantee word access to SRAM.

LF (`\n`) changes itself to CRLF on UART; existing string `\r\n` is not added CR again.
`printf/vprintf` returns the number of logical characters before converting newline. when
encountering unsupported format or UART error, returns `-1`; log header may have been sent.
`neon_console_get_status()` returns `NEON_NOT_SUPPORTED`, `NEON_INVALID_PARAM`, `NEON_BUSY`,
`NEON_TIMEOUT` or corresponding driver error code. A successful call follows a status update; status
is not permanently saved error.

timeout is the budget poll for each UART byte, not milliseconds or deadline of the entire log
stream. Longer logs may take longer to occupy the main. The console rejects a nhau/concurrent nested
call with BUSY; no lock waiting. In FreeRTOS, use mutex or a task log for serialization. In ISR,
give data/events to main/task for processing. If other code also uses that UART or directly calls
`_write`, the application must protect the entire transaction to avoid data interspersal between log
characters.

Format strings and `%s` in SRAM must own all word aligned data, according to `neon_utils_memory.h`.
Buffers that DMA is updating need to be handed over ownership before printing. literal strings in
Flash are read with word aligned. Call printf from main/task after startup/SystemInit. Not used in
reset/ISR before platform ready.

sections.heading: Build and view logs
sections.text:
View the complete project at [examples/Printf_Log](../examples/Printf_Log/README.md). SDK has Serial
Monitor in VS Code; select the correct port, baud 19200 and 8N1 for this example. Can be opened
directly with pyserial:

```sh
python3 -m serial.tools.miniterm /dev/ttyUSB0 19200
```

Connect UART0 TX of the board to RX of USB-UART, general GND; confirm pins and voltage level in
board map. Do not infer 3.3 V/5 V tolerance from UART name. Reset after opening monitor to see boot
log; exit with `Ctrl+]`.

sections.heading: Confirmation Status
sections.text:
Checked build when UART is on/off, format integer 64-bits, line `_write`, initialize UART
automatically, down to CRLF and restore after timeout. Runtime GT32U2086 uses memory access functions in
word 32-bits. No baud, UART pin or log confirmation on real FPGA/silicon.

sections.heading: Documentation organization
sections.text:
The README introduces the SDK, lists prerequisites and provides one initial
build/program workflow. Procedures, architecture explanations and references
are kept in separate guides. This organization draws on how vendors separate
getting-started material from detailed documentation:
[ST · SDK README](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/STM32CubeF4/blob/master/README.md),
[NXP · Getting Started / User Guide](https://mcuxpresso.nxp.com/mcuxsdk/latest/),
[Microchip · Harmony](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/tools-resources/configure/mplab-harmony)
and [Espressif · README](https://github.com/espressif/esp-idf/blob/master/README.md).

sections.heading: Reading the NEON-MDF source
sections.text:
Use a small application such as `examples/Printf_Log` or
`examples/GPIO_Input_Output` to follow the GT32U2086 firmware flow.

sections.heading: From application to hardware
sections.text:
1. Read the application's `Src/main.c`: initialization, terminal, main loop and driver calls.
2. Open the public header in `neon-mdf/components/driver/<peripheral>/` for APIs,
   handles/configuration, return codes and polling budgets.
3. Follow `platform/gt32u2086/neon_<peripheral>.c` for mux, clock/reset, MMIO and critical sections.
4. Compare `mcu-description/devices/GT32U2086.yaml` with the generated header for offsets/bitfields.
5. Use hardware documentation and board measurements to verify timing/IRQ behavior.

sections.heading: From reset to main
sections.text:
`startup_GT32U2086.s` provides vectors and Reset_Handler, initializes `.data`/`.bss`
and calls SystemInit and main. `system_GT32U2086.c` manages clocks and
`SystemCoreClock`. `gt32u2086_runtime.c` provides memory operations suitable for
word-only SRAM. BootROM processes the header and publishes vector information
through the SRAM relay before entering the application.

Generated startup/linker files are in
the application's `build/GT32U2086/generated/GT32U2086/`, with device headers in
its `include/` subdirectory. Source-tree generated files are reference snapshots;
CMake uses the build-local outputs. Edit the YAML/generator to change the output.
See [GT32U2086](GT32U2086.md).

sections.heading: From build to programming
sections.text:
Read `tools/cmake/project.cmake` → `cmake/mcu_variants.cmake` →
`mcu-description/tools/generate.py` → `cmake/kconfig.cmake` →
`cmake/gt32u2086_image.cmake` → `tools/gt32u2086_image.py` →
`cmake/gt32u2086_flash.cmake` → `tools/gt32u2086_flash.py`/`gt32u2086_uart.py`.

[BuildSystem](BuildSystem.md) describes intermediate artifacts and configuration
variables. The CLI/extension call these same targets, so failures can be
reproduced from a terminal.

sections.heading: Checks when changing the SDK
sections.text:
- Match APIs/headers and implementations in types, register widths and lifetime rules.
- Keep linker/startup data and stack allocation out of header/relay reservations.
- Align SRAM buffers and ensure ownership of every accessed word.
- Match actual clocks to UART, timer, I2C and RTOS tick configuration.
- Treat polling budgets as iteration counts, not milliseconds.
- Distinguish host build/link verification from behavior requiring a physical board.

sections.heading: Signing GT32U2086 firmware
sections.text:
Install the optional signing dependency in the Python environment CMake uses:

```sh
python -m pip install cryptography
```

From an application directory such as `examples/Printf_Log`:

```sh
cmake --preset GT32U2086 -DNEON_MDF_SECURE_BOOT=ON
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

Signing uses the ECDSA P-256 private key at `neon-mdf/tools/key.pem` by default.
The bundled key is shared example material for development. Use a separately
managed private key and matching NVR public key for product firmware.
Pass `-DNEON_MDF_SIGNING_KEY=/absolute/path/to/key.pem` to use a different key,
or `-DNEON_MDF_SIGNING_KEY=` to clear a cached override.

The build produces the raw payload, `<app>_image.bin` (unsigned), and
`<app>_image_signed.bin`. With signing enabled, the standard UART flash target
selects the signed image. Reconfigure with `-DNEON_MDF_SECURE_BOOT=OFF` to
return the build and flash workflow to unsigned images.

To sign an existing unsigned internal Flash image from the application directory:

```sh
python ../../neon-mdf/tools/gt32u2086_secure_image.py build/GT32U2086/printf_log_image.bin -o build/GT32U2086/printf_log_image_signed.bin
```

The signing tool verifies its output before replacing the destination.
BootROM v5 uses the fixed signing domain `FU2-IMAGE-V1` and authenticates
internal Flash images against the public key provisioned into NVR. The CMake
flag controls image signing. Provisioning the public key and secure policy is
a separate factory operation. BootROM v5 does not authenticate QSPI XIP images.

`gt32u2086_flash.py --check-only` checks header, size, CRC and vectors. It reports
signature presence but does not read the device NVR key or establish that the
board will authenticate it. Preserve the fixed `FU2-IMAGE-V1` signing domain.
Do not use legacy eFuse/OTP addresses for BootROM v5 security records.

sections.heading: Development environment setup
sections.text:
This guide prepares the tools for building GT32U2086 firmware on Windows, Linux
and macOS. Return to the [README](../README.md) afterward to build and program
your first example. Install the **Arm bare-metal `arm-none-eabi` toolchain** with
newlib; the SDK uses `nano.specs` and `nosys.specs` when linking.

sections.heading: Required tools
sections.text:
| Component | Requirement |
|---|---|
| CMake | 3.25 or later (CMakePresets version 6) |
| Ninja | Available in `PATH` |
| Python | 3.10 or later, with `venv` and `pip` |
| Arm GNU Toolchain | `arm-none-eabi-gcc`, `g++`, `objcopy`, `objdump`, `size`, newlib |
| Git | Clone the SDK |

CMSIS and FreeRTOS-Kernel are included in the repository. Python reads YAML for
code generation, `kconfiglib` handles configuration, and `pyserial` provides UART
access on Windows and automatic port detection. Linux/macOS UART operations use
the Python standard library when the port is specified explicitly.

sections.heading: Linux · Ubuntu/Debian
sections.text:
```sh
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git cmake ninja-build python3 python3-venv python3-pip gcc-arm-none-eabi libnewlib-arm-none-eabi
```

Check `cmake --version`. If your distribution provides a version older than 3.25,
install a suitable version from [CMake](https://cmake.org/download/) and add it
to `PATH`. On other distributions, install equivalent packages or download
[Arm GNU Toolchain](https://developer.arm.com/downloads/-/arm-gnu-toolchain-downloads)
for a Linux host and the `arm-none-eabi` target.

If `/dev/ttyUSB0` or `/dev/ttyACM0` cannot be opened, check the device's owning
group. Ubuntu/Debian commonly require membership in `dialout`:

```sh
sudo usermod -aG dialout "$USER"
```

Log out and back in to apply the new group membership. Close other serial monitors
before programming.

sections.heading: macOS
sections.text:
Install [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/) if needed, then run:

```sh
brew install git cmake ninja python
brew install --cask gcc-arm-embedded
```

The toolchain installation command is documented by [Homebrew Cask](https://formulae.brew.sh/cask/gcc-arm-embedded).

The cask provides Arm GNU Toolchain with its runtime libraries. If downloading
directly from Arm, select the `arm-none-eabi` package for your host architecture
and add its `bin/` directory to `PATH`. Verify both the compiler and `nano.specs`
as described below. UART ports typically appear as `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or
`/dev/cu.usbmodem*`. Install the adapter manufacturer's USB–UART driver if the
operating system does not recognize the device.

sections.heading: Windows · PowerShell or CMD
sections.text:
Install the following components and select the option to add them to `PATH`
where available:

1. [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win).
2. [Python 3](https://www.python.org/downloads/windows/) version 3.10 or later,
   including `pip` and virtual environment support.
3. [CMake](https://cmake.org/download/) version 3.25 or later.
4. [Ninja](https://github.com/ninja-build/ninja/releases): extract `ninja.exe`
   into a directory in `PATH`.
5. [Arm GNU Toolchain](https://developer.arm.com/downloads/-/arm-gnu-toolchain-downloads):
   Windows distribution for `arm-none-eabi`, including newlib.

Open a new terminal after installation. The Python command may be `python`,
`python3` or `py -3`; use the appropriate interpreter to create the virtual
environment. Use `python` after activating `.venv`. Serial ports have names such
as `COM3`; check Device Manager. The README's `cmake -E env` commands work in both
PowerShell and CMD when entered on one line.

sections.heading: Install Python packages in a virtual environment
sections.text:
From the repository root:

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
```

On Windows, replace `python3` with `python` or `py -3` as needed. Activate the
environment using the command for your terminal:

```sh
# Linux/macOS
. .venv/bin/activate
```

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

```bat
:: Windows CMD
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat
```

If PowerShell blocks the activation script, use CMD with `activate.bat`, or invoke
`.venv\Scripts\python.exe` directly and select that interpreter in CMake as shown below.

```sh
python -m pip install -r neon-mdf/tools/requirements.txt
python -c "import yaml, kconfiglib, serial; print('Python dependencies: OK')"
```

The SDK selects its interpreter through `find_package(Python3)`. If you configured
before activating `.venv`, use `--fresh` or select Python explicitly:

```sh
# Run in examples/Printf_Log; replace the path with your .venv interpreter.
cmake --preset GT32U2086 --fresh -DPython3_EXECUTABLE=/absolute/path/to/neon_mdf/.venv/bin/python
```

On Windows, use a path such as `C:/work/neon_mdf/.venv/Scripts/python.exe`.

sections.heading: Verify the environment
sections.text:
```sh
arm-none-eabi-gcc --version
arm-none-eabi-gcc -print-file-name=nano.specs
arm-none-eabi-gcc -print-file-name=nosys.specs
cmake --version
ninja --version
python --version
```

Both `-print-file-name` commands must return existing paths rather than merely
printing `nano.specs` or `nosys.specs`. If either file is missing, install a
toolchain distribution that includes newlib.

```sh
cd examples/Printf_Log
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

The output is `build/GT32U2086/printf_log_image.bin`. A successful build verifies
the compiler → code generation → linking → image packaging workflow. Continue
with [UART programming](GT32U2086Flashing.md) to run on a board. Adapter behavior,
timing and hardware operation must be verified through actual sessions on each
operating system.

sections.heading: SDK environment variable
sections.text:
Bundled examples locate the SDK at `../../neon-mdf`. For a project outside the
repository, set `NEON_MDF_PATH` to the `neon-mdf/` directory:

```sh
# Bash/Zsh, from the repository root
. neon-mdf/export.sh
```

```powershell
# PowerShell, from the repository root
$env:NEON_MDF_PATH = (Resolve-Path .\neon-mdf).Path
```

You can also pass `-DNEON_MDF_PATH=/absolute/path/to/neon-mdf` when configuring.
`export.sh` only sets the SDK path; install the required tools beforehand.

sections.heading: VS Code (optional)
sections.text:
Install [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/), C/C++ and CMake Tools for editor
support. The NEON-MDF extension uses build tools from `PATH`. Node.js with `npm`
is required to build/package the extension from source; see the
[VS Code guide](VSCode.md).

sections.heading: GT32U2086 development in VS Code
sections.text:
NEON-MDF Tools provides serial port selection, an interactive UART monitor,
building, UART programming, menuconfig, debugging and project creation. Complete
[Setup](Setup.md) before running build tasks.

sections.heading: Build and install the extension
sections.text:
If a `.vsix` package built for the current version is available, install it
through **Install from VSIX...**. To build from source, install Node.js with
`npm`, then run from the repository root:

```sh
cd vscode-extension
npm ci
npm run typecheck
npm run compile
npm run vsix
```

The last command creates `neon-mdf-tools-<version>.vsix` using the version in
`vscode-extension/package.json`. In VS Code, open Extensions → the `…` menu →
**Install from VSIX...** and select the generated file. Press `F5`
from the extension project to test in an Extension Development Host. `.vsix`
packages and `dist/` are generated artifacts; rebuild them after extension changes.

For Remote SSH, install the VSIX from the connected SSH window so build and
UART operations use the remote host. Verify the version under **SSH: Installed**
in the Extensions view, then run **Developer: Reload Window** if prompted.
See the [VS Code Remote SSH notes](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/remote/troubleshooting#_need-to-install-local-vsix-on-remote-endpoint).

C/C++ and CMake Tools provide IntelliSense and standard CMake editor support.
Node.js is only needed to develop/package the extension; the installed extension
runs within VS Code.

sections.heading: Open an application
sections.text:
Open the repository or an application folder such as
`examples/GPIO_Input_Output`. Select the **NEON-MDF** icon in the left Activity
Bar to open **Board Tools**, or run **NEON-MDF: Open Board Tools** from the
Command Palette. If the icon is hidden, right-click the Activity Bar and
enable **NEON-MDF**. The **Project** section shows the selected
application, target and SDK path. Click **Application** to choose an app for
this workspace. Until you choose one, commands use the app in the active
editor when possible.

Click **SDK Path** in the sidebar to browse for an SDK on the workspace host or
return to **Auto**. Bundled applications locate the SDK relative to the checkout.
The folder selection is saved for the current workspace. The extension ignores
a default path from another machine if the SDK is missing there.
Use **NEON-MDF: Create New App...** to create a bare-metal or FreeRTOS project.
**Select Target** and **Select Transport** show the supported GT32U2086 preset
and UART transport. VS Code tasks need access to the toolchain and Python environment
described in [Setup](Setup.md).

sections.heading: Build, program and view logs
sections.text:
1. Click **Serial Port** under **Device** and choose the board's UART port,
   such as `/dev/ttyUSB0` on Linux.
2. Under **Actions**, select **Build** to configure with `--fresh` and build the application.
3. Select **Flash via UART** to build as needed and program the image selected by CMake.
   Set boot mode `100` and press RESET when the task reports that UART is ready.
4. Select **Serial Monitor** to open the UART terminal. Type directly into it
   to send characters such as `r` and Enter to the firmware.

**Flash via UART** also configures with `--fresh`, then runs the `flash_uart_gt32u2086` CMake target with the selected
port and flash baud. It sets `NEON_MDF_UART_BYTE_GAP_MS=0` and
`NEON_MDF_UART_LOG=progress`. Follow the task terminal for the reset prompt
and upload progress. The status bar and Command Palette also expose the existing
build and flash commands. The extension carries forward the selected Python
interpreter, memory profile, firmware version and signing options when using
`--fresh`. It resolves the SDK path again on the workspace host.
When no Python interpreter was explicitly configured, the extension looks for
`.venv` in the application, workspace and SDK checkout before letting CMake pick
a system interpreter. Install the SDK dependencies into that environment.
Template `NEON_APP_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ` and `Printf_Log`’s `NEON_PRINTF_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ`
are also retained across fresh configuration.

Flash releases an open monitor session and opens a new one after a successful
upload. **NEON-MDF: Build + Flash + Log** opens the monitor after programming
even if it was closed before the upload. To build and program signed firmware,
configure the application with the options in the [Secure Boot guide](SecureBoot.md).
The extension uses the CMake flash target, which selects the signed artifact
when signing is enabled. To see startup logs again, set boot mode `000` and reset the board with
the monitor open.

| Setting | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `neonMdf.gt32u2086FlashBaudRate` | ROMCODE UART rate, default `19200` |
| `neonMdf.baudRate` | Application UART rate, default `19200` |
| `neonMdf.sdkPath` | Optional SDK path override |

sections.heading: Menuconfig
sections.text:
**Menuconfig** opens the SDK's terminal configuration UI. Save and exit to
regenerate the build configuration. The next build uses the saved `sdkconfig`.

sections.heading: Debug
sections.text:
Install [Cortex-Debug](https://github.com/Marus/cortex-debug) and set up OpenOCD
and GDB for your board. The SDK ships an OpenOCD placeholder. Use adapter and
target files verified for your GT32U2086 board.

Build and program the matching firmware first. Add a configuration like this
to `.vscode/launch.json` in the open workspace folder. The executable path
below assumes you opened `examples/GPIO_Input_Output`. For the repository root,

sections.heading: GT32U2086 examples
sections.text:
Each folder is a separate GT32U2086 application with its own `Src/main.c`, `CMakeLists.txt`,

terminal in its own `Src/main.c` with the prompt `fpga:>>`. Press `r` without Enter to call

When it returns, the terminal waits for `r` again. Build and load a different directory to change

sections.heading: Build one application
sections.text:
Run from the repository root:

```sh
cd examples/SPI_W5500
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

This creates `build/GT32U2086/gt32u2086_spi_w5500` (ELF), `gt32u2086_spi_w5500.bin` (raw payload) and
`gt32u2086_spi_w5500_image.bin` (128-byte GT32U2086 header plus payload). Other directories use the target
name listed in the table. Build directories, configurations and output images are independent.

```sh
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target menuconfig
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
```

Each application keeps its SDK setup, build preset and menu options in its own
`CMakeLists.txt`, `CMakePresets.json` and `Kconfig`.
The default fixed FPGA clock is 10 MHz. `CONFIG_GT32U2086_EXAMPLE_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ` must match the actual
bitstream; choosing a software value does not change the physical FPGA clock.

sections.heading: Load and run
sections.text:
Close the serial monitor before loading. Run inside the chosen application directory,
select boot mode `100`, wait for the loader to report UART ready, then press RESET:

```sh
cmake -E env \
  NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 \
  NEON_MDF_SERIAL_BAUD=19200 \
  NEON_MDF_UART_BYTE_GAP_MS=2 \
  NEON_MDF_UART_LOG=full \
  cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target flash_uart_gt32u2086
```

Use the packaged `_image.bin` when selecting a file manually. After a successful transfer,
ROMCODE hands off to the application. Select boot mode `000` for future resets. Open UART0 at 19200 baud, 8N1, no local echo
and no flow control. Wait for `fpga:>>`, then press `r` without Enter. After `[RUN]`, type the
keys/data shown by that example.
See [GT32U2086 build and boot](../guide/GT32U2086.md) for the ROM boot contract and supported loading methods.

Interactive examples return on their documented stop key; one-shot examples return after completion.
The application then prints `fpga:>>` again. Press `r` to repeat without resetting the board.
While a run is active, its own keys apply: for example, `r` reads SRAM in the SPI/W5500 menu and
arms RX in the UART DMA menu. At `fpga:>>`, Enter starts a new line and displays the prompt again.
CR and LF each work as Enter; a CRLF pair produces only one new prompt. Other unused keys are ignored.

sections.heading: Hardware verification
sections.text:
Read each application's README for pins and remaining hardware limitations. UART DMA retains
its existing word-oriented peripheral profile and timeout-recovery limitations. The TIM1 example
uses live UPDATE status and disables its IRQ if the bounded wait expires; measure timing on the FPGA.
A successful build does not validate physical timing, wiring, interrupt acknowledgement or DMA
handshakes. The SPI/W5500 example needs a matching bitstream/pin route and an attached W5500.

See [hardware support and acceptance checks](../guide/HardwareValidation.md) for capability limits and
required board evidence. The source and automated build checks do not establish hardware validation.

sections.heading: FreeRTOS_Peripheral_Queue
sections.text:
UART RX interrupt and a periodic FreeRTOS task send events to one queue. The terminal
task receives the events during a run, controls **GPIOB7 (PB7)** and prints the results.

This is an independent GT32U2086 firmware. Its UART terminal waits at boot; press `r` without Enter
to start the example at the `fpga:>>` prompt.
The first `r` is received before RTOS initialization. After flashing through UART0,
open the serial monitor and press Enter to redisplay the prompt, then `r`. Startup
logs show peripheral initialization, scheduler startup and terminal task entry.
Console: UART0, 19200 baud, 8N1. FPGA system clock: 10 MHz by default.

Source files are in `Src/`, with the terminal entry in `Src/main.c`. Example headers are in `Inc/`.

`main.c` follows the other GT32U2086 examples, including `GPIO_Input_Output`: print the
banner to initialize the default UART0, borrow its handle with
`neon_console_get_uart()` and check for initialization failure. The terminal loop
is also in `main.c`: print `fpga:>>`, handle Enter/CRLF, wait for `r`, print `[RUN]`,
call `free_rtos_peripheral_queue_run(uart)` and print the prompt again on return.
The first wait for `r` runs before the scheduler starts. Subsequent waits and all
demo runs execute in the terminal task, allowing blocking queue APIs during a run.
There is no separate UART handle or explicit console attachment.

Before starting the scheduler, `free_rtos_peripheral_queue_init(uart)` initializes
PB7, enables the UART FIFO and creates the queue and periodic task once. It waits
for the banner's TX output to finish before updating the existing UART configuration,
as in `UART_RX_Interrupt`. Baud rate and frame format are preserved.

At the prompt the terminal polls UART RX. Once the scheduler is running it yields
for one tick when no byte is available. On `r`, the run function takes over RX using interrupts and consumes the
queue in the same task. Ctrl+C sets PB7 low, disables RX interrupts, discards pending
events and returns to the terminal loop. Polling and ISR never consume RX together.

sections.heading: Hardware
sections.text:
- Connect the board's UART0 console to a serial terminal at 19200 baud, 8N1.
- Observe PB7 with a logic analyzer, or connect an LED with a suitable series resistor.
  Share ground with the board. `1`/`0` mean electrical high/low; LED polarity depends on wiring.
- PB7 is configured as a GPIO output, initially low. Starting or stopping a run also sets it low.
  Periodic events report its state without changing it.

sections.heading: FreeRTOS integration
sections.text:
The build follows `../FreeRTOS_Blinky`: include `neon-mdf/cmake/freertos.cmake`,
call `neon_mdf_add_freertos()` with this application's `Inc/` directory, and link
`freertos_kernel`. The helper selects `GCC_ARM_CM0` and `heap_4` for GT32U2086.
`Inc/FreeRTOSConfig.h` uses `SystemCoreClock`, a 1 kHz tick, an 8 KiB heap and stack
overflow/allocation failure hooks. Software timers are disabled.
`configCHECK_HANDLER_INSTALLATION=0` is required for GT32U2086: Cortex-M0 has no VTOR,
and BootROM v5 forwards interrupts to the application's vector table. The port's
default direct-routing check reads VTOR and can halt before the first task.

```text
UART0 RX FIFO -> USART0_IRQHandler -> xQueueSendFromISR --+
                                                       +-> Event Queue -> run() in terminal task -> PB7 / UART log
Periodic task -> vTaskDelayUntil -> xQueueSend ----------+
```

The queue defaults to 16 events, each containing three aligned `uint32_t` fields:
event type, value and tick timestamp. Values are copied into the queue, which meets
GT32U2086's word-access SRAM requirements without passing temporary buffer pointers.

The periodic task runs at priority 2 with a 128-word stack. It sends an event every
1000 ms while the demo is active; the first event follows the task's existing cadence.
The terminal task runs at priority 1 with a 512-word stack. During a run it blocks
in `xQueueReceive()` when no events are available. Only this task writes console
output after startup.
The producer briefly suspends scheduling around its run-state check and nonblocking
send, preventing a stale periodic send across stop/restart. RX interrupts remain enabled
during this short scheduling suspension when the demo is running.

The scheduler, queue and tasks are created once after the first `r`. Ctrl+C returns from the
run function to its caller in the terminal task; the scheduler keeps running.
Starting again reuses the same objects and resets the run statistics. The Cortex-M0 port does not support
returning to `main()` through `vTaskEndScheduler()`.

sections.heading: Run
sections.text:
At `fpga:>>`, press `r` without Enter to start a run.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `1` | Set PB7 high. |
| `0` | Set PB7 low. |
| `t` | Toggle PB7. |
| `s` | Print processed events, queue-full drops, queued events, PB7 state, free heap and stack high-water marks. |
| Ctrl+C | Stop, discard pending events, set PB7 low and return to `fpga:>>`. |

Example output (tick values and counts depend on input timing):

```text
Press r to run FreeRTOS_Peripheral_Queue (no Enter).
fpga:>> r
[RUN] FreeRTOS_Peripheral_Queue
[READY] queue=16 events, period=1000 ms, output=GPIOB7=0
1=high, 0=low, t=toggle, s=stats, Ctrl+C=stop
[UART] key='1' -> PB7=1
[PERIODIC] seq=1 tick=1000 PB7=1
[UART] key='t' -> PB7=0
```

Both producers use nonblocking queue sends. When full, new events are dropped and
counted separately for UART and periodic events. Periodic sequence gaps can therefore
indicate dropped events. `processed` counts all received demo events, including command
characters and CR/LF; it excludes the start key and the stop signal. Queue-full drops
exclude events deliberately discarded during stop. Stats are snapshots, so new UART
data may arrive while a report is printing.

Ctrl+C is recorded in a separate ISR flag and attempts to enqueue a wake-up event.
If the queue is full the terminal task is already runnable, so stopping does not depend on
free queue space. An in-progress command/log may finish first. Bytes received after
Ctrl+C are drained and discarded until stop completes; wait for `fpga:>>` before `r`.
This protects against software queue overflow; hardware UART overruns can still lose input.

`r` only starts a run when the application is at `fpga:>>`.
At this prompt, Enter starts a new line and prints `fpga:>>` again. CR, LF and CRLF are
supported; CRLF produces only one new prompt.

sections.heading: Configuration and checks
sections.text:
Configure with `cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target menuconfig`, then build again; changes to `sdkconfig` are applied automatically.

| Setting | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CONFIG_GT32U2086_EXAMPLE_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ` | `10000000` | Must match the actual FPGA clock for UART and RTOS timing. |
| `CONFIG_FREERTOS_PERIPHERAL_QUEUE_LENGTH` | `16` | Queue capacity, from 1 to 128 events. |
| `CONFIG_FREERTOS_PERIPHERAL_QUEUE_PERIOD_MS` | `1000` | Periodic interval, from 100 to 60000 ms. |

Suggested hardware checks:

1. Confirm PB7 starts low, then use `r`, `1`, `0`, `t` and check both pin level and logs.
2. Leave the terminal idle during a run: periodic logs continue at the configured interval.
3. Send `10t` in one short burst: commands execute in arrival order if the queue has space.
4. Send a long burst to fill the queue, then `s`: dropped events should be reported.
   Send Ctrl+C during a burst and confirm PB7 returns low and the prompt returns with RX IRQ disabled.
5. Repeat stop/start and `s`: free heap should remain constant; stack-free values are
   lifetime high-water marks and may decrease as new code paths execute.
6. At the prompt, check CR, LF and CRLF; CRLF should produce only one new prompt.

Build success validates compilation, linking and image packaging. Pin routing, UART
interrupt delivery, timing and stack margins still need verification on GT32U2086 hardware.

sections.heading: GPIO_Input_Output

sections.heading: I2C_DMA
sections.text:
Independent GT32U2086 firmware for I2C0 DMA communication with an AT24C256/AT24C256C EEPROM.

This is an independent GT32U2086 firmware. Its UART terminal waits at boot; press `r` without Enter
to start the example at the `fpga:>>` prompt.
Console: UART0, 19200 baud, 8N1. Default FPGA clock: 10 MHz; target SCL: 100 kHz.

Source files are in `Src/`, with the terminal entry in `Src/main.c`. Example headers are in `Inc/`.

sections.heading: Wiring
sections.text:
| FPGA signal | EEPROM signal |
|---|---|
| PMOD_IO6 / package pin 18 | SDA, pin 5 |
| PMOD_IO2 / package pin 19 | SCL, pin 6 |
| Board GND | GND, pin 4 |
| Board-compatible supply | VCC, pin 8 |

SDA/SCL require external pull-ups to the IO supply. Keep WP LOW for writes.
A0/A1/A2 all HIGH select the default 7-bit address `0x57`; other combinations select `0x50..0x57`.
Set `CONFIG_I2C_DMA_ADDRESS` to match the device. The bitstream must route these pins to I2C0
and connect I2C0 TX/RX requests to **DMA1, peripheral slot 4**.

sections.text:
```sh

cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086

  NEON_MDF_UART_BYTE_GAP_MS=2 NEON_MDF_UART_LOG=full \
  cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target flash_uart_gt32u2086
```

releases the port. Use the board's UART-download/normal-boot straps as described in
[GT32U2086 build and boot](../../guide/GT32U2086.md).

sections.heading: Run
sections.text:
Press `r` at `fpga:>>` to run one test:

1. Send EEPROM offset `00 00`, then write the 16-byte pattern `00 01 ... 0F` using TX DMA.
2. Wait at least 6 ms for the EEPROM write cycle.
3. Set the EEPROM read pointer to `0000` using a polling transfer.
4. Read 16 bytes using RX DMA, print them and compare against the pattern.

**Each run overwrites EEPROM bytes `0000..000F` without restoring their previous contents.**
The write fits within one AT24C256 64-byte page. No EEPROM access occurs before `r` is pressed.

A successful run ends with:

```text
[DMA TX] 16 bytes sent; EEPROM write delay complete.
[DMA RX] 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 0A 0B 0C 0D 0E 0F
[VERIFY] 16/16 bytes matched [PASS]
fpga:>>
```

DMA1 channel 0 moves TX data and channel 1 moves RX data in SINGLE mode. Each aligned RAM word
holds one I2C byte in bits `[7:0]`; 16 wire bytes require 64 DMA memory bytes. The two EEPROM
address bytes are queued by the CPU before TX DMA is enabled. The HAL configures the peripheral,
pins and DMA requests; the example programs address/count/direction and START directly because
the HAL has no DMA transaction START API. I2C events are polled without an interrupt handler.
Success requires DMAC completion, peripheral DMA completion, I2C byte-count completion and STOP.

Timeouts and NACKs print the failed stage and I2C status registers. Check the EEPROM address,
pull-ups, WP and bitstream routing. If a DMA command or bus cleanup remains incomplete, the example
retains its buffers and requires an FPGA reset before another run; disabling a DMA channel does
not acknowledge cancellation of outstanding bus accesses.

When the run function completes, the application returns to its UART terminal.
Press `r` again to repeat the example. This is a bounded one-shot test with no inner menu.
At this prompt, Enter starts a new line and prints `fpga:>>` again. CR, LF and CRLF are
supported; CRLF produces only one new prompt.
Configure with `cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target menuconfig`, then build again; changes to `sdkconfig` are applied automatically.
`CONFIG_GT32U2086_EXAMPLE_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ` must match the actual FPGA clock for I2C timing and the write
delay to be correct. `CONFIG_I2C_DMA_TIMEOUT_POLLS` is a polling budget, not milliseconds.
Enable both `CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_I2C` and `CONFIG_NEON_MDF_DRIVER_DMA`.

Building verifies compilation and image packaging. Physical EEPROM behavior, pin routing and DMA
handshakes still require testing on the FPGA.

sections.heading: I2C_EEPROM
sections.text:
Independent GT32U2086 firmware for I2C0 master communication with an AT24C256/AT24C256C EEPROM.
Boot opens the UART terminal at `fpga:>>`. Press `r` without Enter to open the I2C menu.
Console: UART0, 19200 baud, 8N1. Default FPGA clock: 10 MHz; target SCL: 100 kHz.

sections.heading: Wiring
sections.text:
| FPGA signal | EEPROM signal |
|---|---|
| PMOD_IO6 / package pin 18 | SDA, pin 5 |
| PMOD_IO2 / package pin 19 | SCL, pin 6 |
| Board GND | GND, pin 4 |
| Board-compatible supply | VCC, pin 8 |

The bitstream must route PMOD_IO6/IO2 to I2C0. SDA/SCL need external pull-ups to the IO supply.
A0/A1/A2 all HIGH select the default address `0x57`; these pins select addresses `0x50..0x57`. Keep WP LOW
for writes. This example assumes a 32 KiB AT24C256 with a 16-bit memory address and 64-byte pages.

sections.heading: Build and load
sections.text:
```sh
cd examples/I2C_EEPROM
cmake --preset GT32U2086
cmake --build --preset GT32U2086
cmake -E env NEON_MDF_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 NEON_MDF_SERIAL_BAUD=19200 \
  NEON_MDF_UART_BYTE_GAP_MS=2 NEON_MDF_UART_LOG=full \
  cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target flash_uart_gt32u2086
```

The packaged image is `build/GT32U2086/gt32u2086_i2c_eeprom_image.bin`, including the 128-byte GT32U2086 header.
Use the UART-download/boot straps described in [GT32U2086 build and boot](../../guide/GT32U2086.md).
Open the serial monitor after the loader releases the port, with local echo and flow control off.

sections.heading: Menu
sections.text:
Press `r` at `fpga:>>`, then choose one key:

| Key | Operation |
|---|---|
| `s` | Scan all 128 7-bit addresses, `00..7F`; display ACK/NACK map |
| `a` | Write `2A 00` at EEPROM offset `0000`, wait 6 ms, read and compare |
| `r` | Read `0000..00FF` once in four 64-byte blocks, dump 16 bytes per row, return to the menu |
| `t` | Overwrite and verify the first 1 KiB (`0000..03FF`) with a PRNG pattern |
| `q` / Ctrl+C | Stop a long operation after its current block; at the menu, return to `fpga:>>` |

`a` overwrites EEPROM bytes `0000..0001`. **`t` overwrites bytes `0000..03FF` and does not restore
old contents.** Stopping `t` leaves the bytes already written in place. Neither operation runs
automatically at boot or menu entry. The EEPROM capacity remains 32 KiB; these quick tests use
only its beginning.

Scan uses one-byte reads and includes reserved addresses. A scan can advance a device's pointer
or trigger read side effects. ACK identifies an address response and does not identify EEPROM
model/capacity. Read/write tests always use `CONFIG_I2C_EEPROM_ADDRESS`, default `0x57`.
The configured address is not changed by scanning.

A successful two-byte test prints:

```text
[WRITE] mem=0000 data=2A 00; wait 6 ms, then read.
[READ] 2A 00 [PASS]
[MENU] s/a/r/t or q to exit.
```

The write/read test performs 32 writes of 32 bytes without crossing a 64-byte page boundary.
A xorshift32 generator provides a new pattern per run. Each write is followed by a 6 ms delay.
Verification restarts the generator with the same seed and compares all 1024 bytes in sixteen
64-byte reads. It prints the first 64 bytes as a sample and reports the address, expected byte
and received byte for at most eight mismatches. Further mismatches are still counted. The
result includes written/checked byte counts and the total mismatch count; cancellation or a
transport error cannot produce a successful result.

The read command returns to the menu after 256 bytes, cancellation or an I2C error. Transport
errors report the HAL status and the I2C error bitmask. Both tests check `q`/Ctrl+C between
blocks; other received characters are ignored there. The smaller test ranges and limited
UART output keep these examples quick to run.

sections.heading: Configuration and implementation
sections.text:
Open `cmake --build --preset GT32U2086 --target menuconfig`, save, then configure/build again.
`CONFIG_GT32U2086_EXAMPLE_FIXED_CLOCK_HZ` must match the actual FPGA clock. Set the EEPROM address
with `CONFIG_I2C_EEPROM_ADDRESS`; `CONFIG_I2C_EEPROM_TIMEOUT_POLLS` is an iteration budget,
not milliseconds. The driver default calculates standard-mode 100 kHz timing from the
current GT32U2086 clock; the example does not duplicate the timing calculation.

The example calls NEON I2C APIs for all bus transfers. The driver configures clock/reset and
SDA/SCL pin routing. TX preloads up to 32 bytes into the FIFO before START, then streams
the remaining bytes. EEPROM addressed reads use a two-byte pointer write with STOP, followed
by a read with another START/STOP. The last read byte is NACKed by the master. It uses polling;
no I2C ISR or DMA is needed.

During RX, the driver sends STOP when hardware reports transfer DONE, even if the CPU
has not yet copied every FIFO byte to RAM. STOP preserves unread RX data. The driver
then drains the remaining bytes without keeping SCL LOW in the software-end state.

If error bit `NEON_I2C_ERROR_RECOVERY_REQUIRED` (`0x100`) is set, STOP/bus cleanup
did not finish. Further transfers are blocked. Fix the wiring/device holding the bus,
press `q` to close the menu, then `r` to configure I2C0 again.

Application byte values are stored in `uint32_t` elements. Small aligned buffers pack/unpack
these values at the HAL byte-buffer boundary, respecting the GT32U2086 word-only RAM contract.
SysTick runs from the core clock without interrupts for the EEPROM write delay and PRNG seed.
The example requires SysTick to be unused at entry and restores its disabled configuration on exit.

Build/software verification does not establish physical ACKs, clock timing or pin routing.
Run the image with the connected EEPROM to check these on the FPGA.
